speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege-

subtopic: MR. DREW    RELEASE TO PRESS OF CHANGES IN NATIONAL DEFENCE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Again?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MR. DREW    RELEASE TO PRESS OF CHANGES IN NATIONAL DEFENCE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Yes, again, as one hon. member opposite comments. A few days ago I raised a question about an announcement being given to the press with regard to a most important matter affecting all hon. members of this house and their responsibilities as members, and also indicating that it was a departure from the practice adopted only the day before by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Campney) when he did announce in this house certain important changes. I am not proposing to discuss the merits or otherwise of the proposal then made that this should stand until the estimates of the Department of National Defence were under consideration.
Yesterday it was announced that the estimates of the Department of National Defence would be discussed on Thursday, the day after tomorrow, and this morning all of us who have read the press have seen a statement issued by an unnamed official of the Department of National Defence discussing in detail a subject which the government has refused to discuss here. I would point out that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) did not welcome the suggestion that this should have been discussed here at that time. Here this morning is not some casual comment by any member of the press but a report by the Canadian Press giving in quotes a statement issued yesterday by an official of the Department of National Defence in regard to General Simonds' retirement.
If a statement was to be made by the Department of National Defence, as members of this house we had the right to know it and we have the right to know who the official was who gave this statement which is given in quotes in the press today. I would hope that the Prime Minister would also tell us whether that official spoke with the 50433-300
authority of the government, as well as giving us the name of the official who has placed on record a statement which was obviously intended to affect the course of the discussion on Thursday when the estimates of the department come before us.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MR. DREW    RELEASE TO PRESS OF CHANGES IN NATIONAL DEFENCE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member ascertains who the official is, I shall be glad if he will let me know. I do not know. I did not know that the statement was going to be made, and I deprecate these statements attributed to high officials or to official or semi-official sources without disclosing the identity of the one who is communicating the information. I do not think that is a proper course to be followed, and it seems to me that the newspapers themselves would be better advised if they did not take the responsibility of reporting disclosures of that kind when the person making the disclosure is not willing to disclose his own identity. Now, I cannot add any more. I do not think these statements should be made. Had I heard that one was proposed, I would have discussed it with my colleague, the Minister of National Defence, and I am sure we would have agreed that it should not be made. I was curious, as was the hon. gentleman, to know who had made such a statement, and I shall endeavour to find out. If I do, I shall inform the hon. gentleman; and 1 hope that, if he finds out who made it, he will inform me.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MR. DREW    RELEASE TO PRESS OF CHANGES IN NATIONAL DEFENCE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: I would point out, of course, that I have not the same facilities as the Prime Minister to get that information, but I would also point out to the Prime Minister, in case he is not aware of it, that this was issued in the form of a statement handed to the press.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subtopic: MR. DREW    RELEASE TO PRESS OF CHANGES IN NATIONAL DEFENCE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: How do you know?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MR. DREW    RELEASE TO PRESS OF CHANGES IN NATIONAL DEFENCE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: The Prime Minister will be able to ascertain very easily who did that. I welcome the statement of the Prime Minister that he deprecates this practice. The Prime Minister has already indicated that it disturbed him, as it disturbed me, as there is a definite attempt to affect the course of the discussion on Thursday.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MR. DREW    RELEASE TO PRESS OF CHANGES IN NATIONAL DEFENCE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
There was one other matter the hon. gentleman mentioned, that just the day before the announcement was made of the retirement, at some time in the future,

of the chief of staff, there had been a statement made in the house about another officer. The hon. gentleman will remember that this statement was made in response to a question that had been put, I think, on the Friday, and the minister had promised to make it. The hon. Leader of the Opposition himself asked me for a statement about it. My reply was that the Minister of National Defence and I had discussed it and that the Minister of National Defence was going to make a statement. Whenever we are asked for information, we do our best to supply it, but it has not been the practice to announce in the house the appointments of deputy ministers, though they are made by order in council. It has not been the practice to make announcements in the house of changes in command in the defence department, but whenever there is any question asked about them we endeavour to supply full information.

I understand that it is not in nearly as complete detail as the statement which was actually handed out. Since the Prime Minister has indicated his desire to answer questions, at this time I am asking the question as to who the official is that issued this statement to the press, and under whose authority.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS AT GENEVA-TABLING OF DOCUMENT SHOWING CONCESSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for the information of hon. members I wish to make an announcement about some tariff negotiations which have recently been concluded in Geneva. These negotiations have been carried out under three headings, first, for the accession of Japan to the general agreement on tariffs and trade, second, to give effect to the desire of some other countries to renegotiate certain increases in tariff rates bound under the general agreement; and third, to renegotiate increases in certain Canadian tariff rates which are bound to other countries under the agreement.
I am tabling a document showing the concessions on both sides and the withdrawal of earlier concessions resulting from negotiations. This shows the concessions to the exchange by Canada with Japan and the United States. It also sets forth the compensation given by the United States for the

withdrawal of the concession on flshsticks. My colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) announced on June 2 changes in the Canadian tariff resulting from the renegotiation of two items which had been bound by Canada. In order to give a complete picture these are also mentioned in this document which I am about to table. The results of our tariff negotiations with Japan, and some related negotiations with the United States, will not become effective before the end of the summer. In general, the changes involved are not very extensive from our point of view. With your consent, Mr. Speaker, I would ask that the document which I now table be published as an appendix to Hansard.

maintopic: SECOND REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON PROCEDURE
subtopic: REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE
speechtext:
I have the honour to present the second report of the special committee appointed to consider with Mr. Speaker the procedure of this house, in both English and French.
The report of the special committee on procedure which I have just tabled contains quite a number of minor changes in the rules and the practice of the house. It also contains several quite important changes in the rules. In order that hon. members may have a ready reference to what has been recommended, perhaps a short statement might be useful.
1.	It is recommended that the house sit on Friday mornings from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m. and adjourn at 6 p.m. Otherwise, the hours of sitting remain the same and the weekly working hours are the same as at present.
2.	There is a new provision for the answering of starred questions on Wednesdays, namely, it is proposed to devote up to one hour on Wednesdays to answering questions orally. Questions may also be answered in writing; and returns and other papers tabled as at present, except that they are to be deposited with the Clerk and they will be shown as at present in the Hansard or Votes and Proceedings.
3.	The principal changes consist of restricting the length of speeches in committee to 30 minutes; and restrictions on the debate on

the address in reply to the speech from the throne; the debate on the motion to go into committee of supply and of ways and means; and on private members' days.
4.	The debate on the address is limited to 10 days, with provision made for voting on subamendments and amendments on the sixth and ninth days.
5.	Six motions to go into committee of supply are to be made on Mondays and the debate is limited to the two days of Monday and Tuesday, with provision for voting on amendments not later than 8.15 p.m. on the second day. However, if the full two days be not taken on any motion, there is provision for adding the unused time to subsequent motions. The Speaker shall leave the chair without question put for the purpose of going into committee of supply on Wednesdays as well as on Thursdays and Fridays as at present.
6.	The budget debate is limited to eight days, with provision for voting on the subamendment and the amendment on the fifth and seventh days; on all other motions when going into committee of ways and means, Mr. Speaker shall leave the chair without question put.
7.	Private members' days are limited to the first six Mondays and the first two Thursdays after the conclusion of the debate on the address, but any of these Mondays may be used for a supply motion; and if so used, the private members' days will be deferred.
As I have said, there are a number of incidental changes both in rules and practice, having in mind that this is the first revision of the rules of any consequence in many years.
I should like to advise the house that this report is unanimous. I think I may say that the report is the product of hard work on the part of members of the committee. Special credit is due to the members of the subcommittee consisting of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris), the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton), the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch), assisted by the Clerk and the second clerk assistant.
I beg leave to advise further that all members of the committee feel that the report ought to commend itself to the house.

speechtext:
Before it is adopted, Mr. Speaker, I should like to know if the person who has been in charge of the index for some time will be the head of the body of people who will look after the index. I have no grudge against anybody but, as I have said before, I remember the time when we received an unbound copy of the index for the whole session 15 days after prorogation or 15 days after the house had adjourned for a long period of time. While your predecessor performed your functions, Mr. Speaker, I made many protests about the lateness of the delivery of the Hansard index to the members. I had the vocal support of some members, and finally, after numerous protests, we received a copy of the index. If it was done right for a number of years under a different staff, there is no reason now for such a delay. I wonder what improvements there will be in the organization so far as the making and delivery of the index to Hansard is concerned.
I took the trouble to telephone the printing bureau, and I was told it was not the fault of the printing bureau that there was delay in receiving the index but it was because they had not received the copy on time. The work must be done daily and members should have the opportunity to consult the index daily. The work was done by two ladies in the first place and was done very well. I remember that when I needed information about the date of a speech or the date of an answer to any question I could go to the Hansard office and get that information at once. Naturally the cards could not be taken out of the office but we were able to examine all the cards there and find the information right away. The work was well done. I hope that under the new arrangement the work will also be well done.
With regard to research, I am not strong for that for the very good reason that I have done my own research and my parliamentary work for 31 years without the assistance of any bureaucrats and any people with long hair and big goggles. I have done my work myself. If there are new members who come

Hansard Index
in and who want to make extensive research they have only to go to the library where the staff is most competent and most obliging. They have been most helpful to me, even under most difficult circumstances. At the moment they have only part of the books in this building that belong to the parliamentary library. They get them from the supreme court library and they give them to us. They are most helpful. I have never heard any complaint from anyone in the library when I asked them to find some reference book for me.
What can happen under the new system? We will have the intelligentsia preparing members' speeches. We will have doctors of philosophy, Ph.D.'s, etc., etc., preparing fine speeches like the ones we have heard from the opposition on the Defence Production Act. There will be quotations from all sources, unknown to the majority of people and interesting no one. They will quote Cripps, Morrison and everyone; there will be no end to it. This suggestion, Mr. Speaker-

May I just answer at this moment questions which have already been asked by the hon. member for Temiscouata. His protests on many matters have often borne fruit. One of the purposes of this motion is to provide for a reorganization of the staff so that the
[Mr. Pouliot.l
index work may be done more quickly and be of more value to hon. members. That is the sole purpose of it.

maintopic: APPROVAL OP REPORT OP CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION RESPECTING STAFF
speechtext:
I thank the minister for what he has said. I want to bring to your attention, sir, that if we have a competent staff to prepare an index that is understandable and that is complete, there will be no use in anyone conducting research to tell a member how to use the index. Anyone who is elected to the House of Commons is supposed to be intelligent enough, even if he is not a graduate of any university, to know how to use an index and how to use a reference book.
We have reference books here, and the first one is the Parliamentary Guide which is supplied to all members. It is up to date, and it is a very useful book. It gives us an opportunity of knowing all about the accomplishments of each one of us. We know all sorts of interesting things, the things that members think most important to write in their autobiography. Our autobiography is like a conversation with a member. It tells about his wife and his children, where he was born, where he has been to school, how long he has been mayor of his community and so on. It is a book that is easy to look at.
And there is another document which is very important, and that is the plan of the house, because it indicates the constituency for which each member sits. Then, if you have the parliamentary guide and the plan of the house you know that Mr. So-and-So, in the background, Mr. John Doe, is the distinguished member for this constituency, of this province in Canada. You have the Parliamentary Guide and you know all about his accomplishments about which you want to be informed. The same applies to the senators and high civil servants.
Then, there is Votes and Proceedings which tells us about the accomplishments of the house on the preceding day. Then we also have Orders of the Day, which are the agenda of the present sitting day. How many members read it, I do not know. But they are made available to us, and are graciously put on our desks.
Then there is Hansard. Hansard is a confused mass of statements that are impossible to find unless there is a good index, and that is why I appreciate the index very much.
Then there are other books which are read by no one, but which are most interesting. Sometimes I read them, because I am quite sadistic in that I read books no one else reads. Then there are departmental reports, thick books. I presume anyone who knows how

to read and write can see those books and find out what he wants to know about any department of government.
And there are the Public Accounts, which complete the reports of the departments; because in the reports of the departments the names of civil servants are not mentioned, and the numbers of positions are not mentioned. We find that information in the public accounts. That library is at the disposition of all of us, and it is in both languages. Those who do not know English may use the French copy, and those who do not know French may use the English; and then everybody can be happy.
It is the finest organization. No company, no other organization has it. What is the use of having research people to embarrass members by putting wrong ideas in their heads, and making them false doctors, a lot of them. Imagine what the house will be like when we have doctors in the house, doctors in all sorts of sciences, who would prepare speeches. It is done, actually, to a certain extent. But imagine what it would be like if each member were supplied with someone who would take him by the hand, just the same as Virgil took Dante to visit the inferno.
Well, sir, I am all for the simple life. I am for simplicity in dealing with my fellow members. When I have something to say to a member, I ask him. Even if his autobiography is not complete, I will write to him to ask him on what precise day he was born.
I shall not insist any more upon it. But I do not believe in the streamlining of parliament and in the rationalization of parliament. We have lived together quite happily for a long time without all these frills and I hope that we will become more simple-mannered and use the old ways of discussion. By the way, I want to congratulate all hon. members upon having done so well and I do not see how they can do any better with the assistance of Ph.D's, beards, long hair and black goggles.

speechtext: the third reading of Bill No. 328, respecting unemployment insurance.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE BENEFIT RATES, ADJUST CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill has had exhaustive consideration by the standing committee on industrial relations and also by the committee of the whole on Friday last. On both occasions members of this group indicated their disapproval of some half dozen amendments which are being made to the act, meanwhile agreeing in general with the provisions set out in Bill No. 328. However, having attempted on several occasions to have the bill amended in various ways and having met with little success in any of our suggestions we now arrive at the third reading of this bill after which in effect it will become the new Unemployment Insurance Act.
I think it would be well if all hon. members of the house were to consider the basis of the fund administered by the commission under the authority of the Department of Labour and to consider for a moment that in the main this fund is built up through contributions by employers and employees. True, there are also contributions from the tax revenues of this land; but generally speaking about 85 per cent of the money in the fund is placed there through contributions by workers of this country and the employers who give them work.
The one requirement of Bill No. 328 to which we took the most objection was the reduction of the maximum benefit period from 51 to 30 weeks. In considering this bill it was brought out by the government and by the government supporters that the bill comes into effect on October 2. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it is not a measure about which there is any great urgency. The government, by its own wish, has deferred the effective date until the autumn of this year, presumably so that it will be in plenty of time for whatever may occur in the coming winter season.
It is also provided in the bill, with particular respect to this section to which we have taken exception, that there shall be a transitional period of some three years, during which time those workers who have built up by their contributions a sizeable fund will not suffer by reason of the reduction to the 30-week period, a period which has now of course been extended to 36 weeks after the representations which were made by the members of the committee and by members of this house. I think we might very well ask ourselves why it was considered necessary to reduce these benefits to 30 weeks and now to 36 weeks. It should not have been because of the drain on the fund, although in the introductory remarks which the minister made and which were repeated on different occasions there was reference

to a drain on the fund. But I would point out that the actuary's own figures do not indicate that any such drain is anticipated. As a matter of fact, I quoted figures when we were considering this bill in committee of the whole on June 10. At that time, having pointed out the figures which I had taken from the report of the actuary, I made this observation, which I should like to repeat. This is on page 4626 and 4627 of Hansard of June 10, 1955:
It is my opinion that after these new provisions have been in effect for a year the fund will be even healthier than it is today. I base that opinion on the fact that, from the actuary's own calculations, there is every expectation of a net profit.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to explore for a few minutes the possible thinking which resulted in the reduction of this maximum period. At page 4626 of Hansard I quoted from the report which had been made by the commission, in which these words appear:
In view of the high percentage of claimants who do not use the long period ... it was considered justified to reduce the maximum period of entitlement to 30 weeks.
It was considered justified, so the report said. I should like to ask hon. members in this house to consider just what constitutes that justification. Was it monetary considerations? I think not, because, as has been shown and as I have referred to the actuary's report, there was no substantial drain anticipated on the fund. Now that the period has been increased from 30 weeks to 36 weeks, by the minister's own admission, the number of claimants who will be cut off from the additional period are 1-75 per cent of all claimants. So there can really be no justification from the monetary standpoint. Was the justification one of ease of administration? Well, possibly. In fact, I might go further and say that probably that had as much to do with it as anything.
The fact that a certain number of people could be eliminated from benefit at a definite time would probably thin the ranks of those seeking benefits and likewise of those seeking employment. But in any of these considerations, did the human element enter in? I do not think we can say other than definitely not. The human element did not enter into the consideration of the reduction to 36 weeks, as it now stands. True enough, as has been mentioned in this house and in committee, the minister made reference to the forthcoming conference which will seek to establish between the federal and provincial authorities some responsibility for relief payments to those persons who are unemployed and employable and not eligible for unemployment insurance benefits. I repeat the
Unemployment Insurance Act word "relief", which has been bandied around -"unemployment relief". I say once more that the average person who has been employed over a period of time cannot qualify for unemployment relief, unless he has first of all used up whatever funds he may have saved and liquidated his more liquid assets and in turn used those up. Then, when he finally has become destitute, he may be eligible for unemployment relief. In my estimation this is not good enough. The fact that even 1-75 per cent of claimants could benefit for an additional period is quite sufficient justification, to use the term used in the report, for reconsideration of this point.
I had a letter, which came to my desk just this morning, from a worker in Toronto who asks some very pertinent questions. He points out that when in April a certain number of people are cut off from supplementary benefits they are told that after they have the required number of contributions to their credit as shown by the stamps placed in their books, they will once more be eligible for benefits. He asks a very pertinent question: How does one go about getting these benefits? How does one go about securing jobs when one is told repeatedly at the unemployment insurance offices that there are no jobs? How can one take a realistic view of the advice which is given to workers out of employment, cut off from supplementary benefits, that they should secure work and accumulate sufficient contribution indications to permit them to qualify again, when the very office which tells them to secure employment knows it cannot supply them with jobs? This situation becomes progressively worse as the worker becomes older. This worker who wrote to me also draws attention to the fact that after 14 days, if the claimant has not appeared at the unemployment insurance office, he is stricken from the list of those seeking work. It is assumed that he has found employment. Hence the statistics of persons seeking work are reduced by the number of people who have lost heart and have given up applying at the national employment service for employment. Then the newspapers spread the glad tidings that things are not as bad as they were, and that they are greatly improved. I admit that at the present time things are greatly improved and I am mighty glad of it; but I still say that there are a great many of these people who have lost heart because they could procure no employment at the national employment service and who, instead of wasting hours standing in line when they know the case is hopeless, have gone out on their own to find whatever work is available in order

Unemployment Insurance Act to earn a little bit of money, whether they do it in employment which is insurable or not.
The minister himself must have been aware that hardship would ensue from these regulations. Speaking in the house the other day, as reported at page 4647 of Hansard, he had this to say:
The hon. member for Hamilton West may say, "Well, you put that in, hut you are not quite sure. You just want to have a trial run".
Then the minister said this:
X will agree that this is a cautious and conservative-with a small "c"-step; I will admit that at once. But it is a cautious and conservative step just to make sure that these people the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has been referring to will not suffer any hardships during that period of time. If they do suffer hardship, then we will do something about it.
Hence the minister himself has anticipated that there may be hardship arising out of this change in the act. In the remarks which he made at that time, following on those which I have just quoted, he referred to the fact- which I mentioned a few minutes ago-that 1 [DOT] 75 per cent of claimants will be all that could be left out now that the period has been increased to 36 weeks. Then he goes on, and in this I may say he picked up my own phrase which I had used on two or three occasions, namely "a trial run", to say once more:
This is a cautious, conservative trial run for the next three years. Before that three years is up the act will certainly be gone over very carefully.
But I should like to draw the attention of this house, Mr. Speaker, to the fact that even if the act is gone over very carefully, opinion will be weighted against the 1 [DOT] 75 per cent of claimants for the reason that we shall then have this 36 weeks' limitation in the act which will by then have been in force for three years and will be one which it will not be easy to change. I draw attention further to the fact that this 1-75 per cent of claimants who will be cut off after the 36-week period will be the very ones who will be in the most dire need of benefit.
I make a plea to this house to consider the fact that, while under our system of government it is true that the majority rules, it is also true that it is our duty as members of this house never to forget that one of the reasons we are here is to protect the rights of minorities. The fact that there are so few who are expected to be affected under this change in the act is all the more reason why they should not be thrown into the discard.
I maintain what I said before, Mr. Speaker, namely that the government is not sure, the minister is not sure and the commission is
[Mrs. Fairclough.j
not sure. It is a case of the blind leading the blind. I do not like this reduction. At the very start when we were at the resolution stage and when an indication was given to us that this reduction would be made, I said we would fight this proposal to the very last ditch. I hope I was wrong when I said we would fight it; I hope that the acting minister will acquiesce-as was indicated the other evening in the house that he possibly might- and restore this period to 51 weeks. Let the transitional period be one in which they will consider whether there should be a reduction, not one in which they will consider whether or not the period should be restored to its previous level.
Mr. Speaker, I plead for this 1-75 per cent of claimants. I once more draw attention to the fact that the fund belongs to the contributors, at least to the extent of 85 per cent; and even those contributors are among the taxpayers who contribute the other 15 per cent. It is their fund. It has not been shown that there will be any drain on the fund. Even if there were, in my estimation it is for this house to consider how that extra expenditure can be met. There is no relief for the workers despite the plan to share unemployment relief with the provinces. There is to be considered the uncertainty of this government with regard to this particular clause; as shown in the reduction from 51 weeks to 30 weeks and then to 36 weeks; and the establishment of a transitional period "if there is hardship," in the minister's own words. The act does not go into force, as I said before, until October 2. This is not a bill which needs to be rushed through because of imminent problems. We can take all the time we need to consider this particular point. The government is in no hurry to put the bill into effect. Apparently, judging by its own effective date, it is trying to get it into effect only before next winter. Therefore, having regard to all of these points, I move:
That Bill No, 328 be not now read a third time but be referred back to the committee of the whole for the purpose of reconsidering clause 48 (1) (a).

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE BENEFIT RATES, ADJUST CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this time, on third reading, I do not think it is necessary to go into a long debate on this bill. It is a bill that has had fairly thorough examination. I think most of the members in the house who felt responsibility for it-I refer to those who were on the committee-have already put on the record their opinions and ideas with regard to the bill. In view of the move to refer the bill back to committee of the whole, it is rather unfortunate that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) is not here. During the course of the

discussion in the standing committee the particular section dealing with the period of 51 weeks was pretty thoroughly chewed over. The hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) moved that the period of 30 weeks fixed in the original bill be changed to 36 weeks, indicating that the Minister of Labour was perhaps inclined to be a bit flexible about the matter. At that time the members of this group put themselves on record with regard to the question of 51 weeks. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) moved an amendment to the motion of the hon. member for Spadina that the period of 51 weeks should be continued instead of having a period of 36 weeks. We tried to get an amendment.
Despite the fact we were reasonably sure the period was going to be 36 weeks, when the members of the committee were drafting their final report they left the matter open. We said that further consideration should be given to expanding the period beyond 36 and up to 51 weeks. Therefore the hon. member is not moving anything new. Several different motions were made in the standing committee and then there was the recommendation in the committee's report.
Of course our position is that we will vote for the amendment. It is the kind of bear trap that you have to vote for, considering the circumstances in which the amendment is moved, regardless of whether it is good, bad or indifferent. But I should like to say as briefly as I can that while my hon. friend's argument capitalizes on the unfortunate unemployed, I have yet to hear a suggestion from that group as to what might be done about the matter. Unemployment insurance is not an end in itself, and does not bring about any finality under the present scheme of things. That is clearly recognized in the United States, and they are doing something about the matter.
As I have pointed out a good many times, the government does not make employment or create unemployment in the field in which my hon. friends are arguing or in the field where this legislation is designed to help, not to cure. As I have said before, there is the question of technological advances and automation in every industry in the country from fishing right through to the appliance plants. There is not an industry in Canada, or in North America for that matter, that is not going through that process and will continue to do so. As the production machine is perfected and more and more labour-saving devices are used, you are going to have more and more unemployment.
This type of legislation is not going to change the situation. As I said before, it is 50433-301
Unemployment Insurance Act not an end in itself that will take care of unemployment in the future. It is merely a supplementary piece of legislation that eases the burden for a given period, and that is all it is.
I think we in this house should come down to earth and try to show employers that they have a social responsibility as well as economic authority. Having a social responsibility, they are going to have to devise ways and means of taking care of human beings who are displaced by machines. That is the road ahead. It is not good enough to say that we are going to pass the Unemployment Insurance Act. That will simply give the man or woman unemployed a certain number of months of unemployment insurance, and then if there is not employment for them they will be on the road. That is not good enough. There has to be something in addition to the Unemployment Insurance Act, and I think the United States is on the right track. The employers and the unions in the case of General Motors and Ford have worked out a means whereby the employees will have a pay envelope 52 weeks of the year.
The guaranteed annual wage as worked out by Ford and General Motors is merely a supplementary wage to unemployment insurance. They are linked now. Unemployment insurance supplements the guaranteed wage up to the figure that has been arrived at through the processes of their collective bargaining machinery. That is something to which thought must be given in Canada. We must not simply keep on thinking in terms of embarrassing the government by making a motion to amend a completely inadequate piece of legislation so far as unemployment is concerned. It is only a stop-gap, merely a palliative. It is a patch on the hull of the old ship that is pretty well scuttled today when you think in terms of the 1930's or even the 1940's. We are not living in that kind of world any more and we had better begin to recognize it.
I do not say that the guaranteed annual wage can be brought about in any industry overnight. There are many industries to which I do not think it is adaptable, but it is something about which we have to begin to think. Employers will have to share their equal responsibility in the field of unemployment because we cannot help the new gadgets that are coming into use. If you examine every industry in the country over the past ten years you will see the same trend. One-half the number of miners in the United States are producing twice as much coal as was produced ten years ago. That is true right along the line. It is true of the appliance industry, the automobile industry, every

Unemployment Insurance Act industry in the country, even agriculture. The fishing industry is being mechanized today. The old type of fisherman is disappearing from the waters and is being replaced by trawlers.
We have to begin to think in terms of those in the field of employment accepting a social responsibility for those replaced by machines. As far as I can see there are only two ways you can do it. First of all, we will have to think seriously about the question of a supplementary payment from the employer while the employee is out of work. The second is the question of a reduction in the hours of labour. Responsible people in the labour movement who have watched the technological trend over the past 50 years have recognized that sooner or later something has to be done with regard to a reduction in the hours of labour if the maximum number of people are to have employment and man is to derive benefit from the introduction of machines.
These are two practical considerations that I think we must face. We will vote for the amendment, but it is only a gesture. Everybody in the house could vote for it. We would all prefer to see a period of 51 weeks rather than 36 weeks, and the cost would not be so great. If it is going to be 36 weeks rather than 51 weeks there will be a wider area of unemployment. There is no doubt about that. Men are going to cease receiving benefits that much sooner and become a charge on the municipalities. We pointed that out. I got a sore throat doing it. The federal and provincial governments are talking about some formula to provide unemployment relief. The word "relief" should never be used.
As far as the government of Nova Scotia is concerned, I know they are not thinking in this way. A few days ago the premier of that province stated' that as far as he was concerned the government would not go along with anything that suggested a return to the conditions of the 1930's. He said that if the federal and provincial governments are going to spend money to relieve the unemployment situation it should be spent in such a way as to create jobs. I think he is going to insist on that when he comes to the next conference, and I hope he does. So far as the resources of that province are concerned, there are things that need to be done. If money is to be available on a contributory basis as between the different governments, let us develop these resources and put people to work rather than have them rot on relief. But as I said before, there is no use in just talking about these things and paying lip service to them.


I want to point this out. Previous to the adoption of this act, there was a regulation that prohibited any supplementary payments from unemployment insurance to a plant that had a guaranteed annual wage. This regulation is dead. It died when this act came into force. I am glad the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) is piloting the bill at the moment. He comes from a town that is close to the border, a town where this guaranteed annual wage is going to be a live issue within the near future. I have known him a long time, and I know the minister is just as realistic in so far as the annual wage is concerned as I am. I know that he will use his influence to see that regulation is not re-enacted. This question of supplementary payments, in so far as the unemployment insurance commission and industries in this country are concerned, should be left open until such time as some formula is worked out. They had to do it in the United States, and we may have to do it here to face up to this question of unemployment.
Unemployment is not seasonal any longer. Largely it is a product of improved machinery and plant. As they improve, we are going to have more and more unemployment. The group about which I am concerned in this 36 to 51-week period is the older men. They are being pensioned off at 65 years of age, and what pensions! If we had been smart in this country, and do not make any mistake about it, I advocated this 30 years ago, we would have had a decent industrial pension plan on a contributory basis in every plant in Canada. But in the early years that was resisted by employers. Today in some industries we have pensions that average about $35 per month at 65 years of age. Hundreds of the men who are being laid off at that age are just as fit for work as they were 15 years before. When they get that pittance of a pension, they register for further employment, but they are over 40 and they cannot find employment in industry.
I want to make this point very clear. It is the policy of every industry in this country today not to hire men over 40 years of age. This arises out of the fact that, too late, they have put in contributory pension plans and when a man is over 40 they do not want him in that plan because he is not going to pay into it long enough to provide for the amount he will get when he retires. We have to realize that these are factors. In my judgment this group is the product of the machine age. They are being thrown out at that age because of the shortsightedness of both governments and industries across this country. I never believed that the people who

pioneered the labour movement in this country had any more brains than anyone else, but 30 years ago I was saying a lot of the things outside of this house that I am saying here now. Year after year since the industrial revolution there have been improvements in machinery. The only answer I could ever see was something along the lines of the guaranteed annual wage, a shortening of the hours of labour, and instead of the piecemeal industrial pensions that we have today, which only create problems, there should be a national retiring allowance on a contributory basis for everybody in this country.
In this way we could provide a decent pension for people who are retiring at 65 years of age. It could be made uniform to cover everyone in the country. Several million dollars a year in expenses could be saved because of the duplication in administration from plant to plant, and that sort of thing. The machinery to handle a national retiring allowance is set up now in the form of the annuities branch. There should be one payment such as we make now under the old age security plan. Take it out of taxation, and make the pension adequate. No one in this country will object to that, least of all those who can see the end of the road at 65 and who have never made enough money to enable them to save very much. They would be saving if the matter were handled in that way.
I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, that I have taken more time than I intended. When I get thinking of this kind of problem, I run on and on. I should like to say we will support this amendment, and I trust that during the period between the passing of the bill and October 2, the effective date, the government can examine the report of the committee in respect to this particular amendment and see if something cannot be done to prevent a widening of the area of unemployment until such time as there is a formula worked out whereby other legislation may be able to handle the problem.

speechtext:
We in this group intend to support the amendment. Of course, as we have stressed time and again, unemployment insurance is not a solution to unemployment. I recall that during the last election the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) stressed the fact that international tension was lessening and as international tension lessened the defence expenditures could be reduced and the standard of living in the country would rise. Yet today, we find that the situation is in many respects quite serious. It was very serious last winter. Whilst unemployment has lessened somewhat 50433-301J
Unemployment Insurance Act now, you would nevertheless expect that in the month of June employment would be at its peak. There should be practically no problem of unemployment.
The big problem, as we see it, is that we have built up this tremendous productive capacity which enables industry today to turn out goods at a considerably greater rate than the people of the country are able to consume them, not at a faster rate than the people want to consume them but at a faster rate than they are able to consume them because they lack the wherewithal to buy them. In spite of the fact the people of Canada today are going into debt at an exceptionally fast rate in order to acquire the goods they want, we are not able to maintain an effective demand for our production. I mention the fact we are going into debt at a heavy rate because charge accounts and buying on the instalment plan are up around the figure of $1,800 million. In addition to that, people have gone into debt under the National Housing Act, the Farm Improvement Loans Act and various other acts to the tune of several hundred millions of dollars.
In spite of the fact that in order to buy the goods they need people are going so heavily into debt, we are still unable to maintain an effective demand for our production. Consequently, when industry is unable to sell its total production and is forced to curtail its production, it helps to expand unemployment. We feel therefore that whilst unemployment insurance is necessary to help provide assistance to those people who are unemployed, nevertheless it must be the responsibility of the federal government to provide a greater degree of employment in this country. We feel that one step should have been to reduce the sales tax which would have helped to expand the purchasing power of the people. We feel the government should take full responsibility for all assistance to the unemployed-and in this I include assistance to all those who are not receiving assistance under the Unemployment Insurance Act.
Further, we feel the government should be prepared to institute national projects to take care of those who are unemployed and cannot be absorbed by industry. It seems a fantastic situation to find throughout this country, where there are so many services required, such large numbers of unemployed, and to find that in these circumstances the government is not prepared to put projects into operation to provide those services the people require. I should imagine one could go into any community anywhere in Canada and find services required by the people.

Unemployment Insurance Act
We have large scale unemployment, and yet the federal government refuses to take the steps necessary to provide those services. In the west we need irrigation projects; we are still short of roads, and we have many level railroad crossings. Yet we have this unemployment problem, one that would disappear overnight if the federal government were prepared to give the necessary financial assistance to the provinces and the municipalities to provide these services.
Then we come to agriculture. We believe a sound program of support prices would help expand the purchasing power of the farmer, and would help also to provide a market for the products of the eastern manufacturer. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) pointed out in his budget speech that the recession, if one may so describe it, was due largely to a drop in farm income. By increasing farm income through adequate support prices we would help to maintain the domestic market.
Then, we feel the federal government is falling down badly in the matter of international trade. Through its pig-headedness on the question of the acceptance of foreign currencies, we are allowing the United States steadily to take our markets from us. And until such time as we are prepared to compete with nations such as the United States on the terms I have suggested, we will continue to lose markets.
Let me say in closing that while we will support the amendment and while we realize the need for strengthening the Unemployment Insurance Act we believe this is not a solution to the problem at all. The solution is in finding ways and means of giving employment to the people.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, rising at this time to say a few words on this bill, I do so to support the amendment submitted by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fair dough). At the outset may I point out to the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) that this amendment is the result of sound and logical reasoning, and a view shared not only by this party but also, may I point out to him, by the workers in Canada and by the labour leaders who have the welfare of the workers so much at heart.
The new bill is a good one, and has many acceptable features. Certainly it is more understandable than the old act. The Progressive Conservative party is in favour of this new measure, with one exception, and that is the exception covered by the amendment which was moved this morning. The reduction from 51 weeks to 30 weeks has


again been amended to 36 weeks. That alone proves that the reduction to 30 weeks was not based upon any sound reasoning. This is borne out by the fact that reconsideration has been given to the matter, and it has been amended to 36 weeks. Under those circumstances, Mr. Speaker, there is no reason why it should not remain at the old maximum of 51 weeks of benefit. If it did it would offer a safety valve for a time when serious unemployment might occur in Canada.
It could be argued that after 36 weeks anyone who was still unemployed would receive the benefits of unemployment relief. To my mind that is not the answer because it would not compare by any means with the $30 a week provided in the bill by way of unemployment insurance. It would be far short of that amount.
It is argued that with maximum benefits at 51 weeks there might be the possibility that during a serious time of unemployment the insurance fund would become impaired. If we look at the fund from 1942 to 1955 we find that at no time was it seriously impaired. We see that it has increased gradually at the rate of about $70 million a year, with one exception when in one year it increased only to the extent of $30 million. To my mind, therefore, there is no danger of serious impairment of the fund, even if the maximum period of 51 weeks were placed in the act.
For these reasons I feel the clause should be reconsidered and the amendment should be accepted by the government and placed in the new measure. This to my mind is very important. It has been urged by labour leaders and workers, that there seems to be no sound reason why it should be reduced. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) himself stated in committee that in the past only a very small percentage have availed themselves of the full maximum of 51 weeks.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE BENEFIT RATES, ADJUST CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak for just a few minutes. As the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) has pointed out, we shall support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Hamilton West. It deals with what we feel is one point in the revised act where a retrograde step has been taken. There are quite a number of places where we feel forward steps should have been taken, but which the government has failed to take. In this instance, however, it is our view that a backward step has been taken, and we deplore it as strongly as we can.
We interpret-and I am sure we are correct in this-a vote for this amendment to refer the bill back to committee of the whole for

the purpose of reconsidering clause 48(1) (a) as support for the proposition that the maximum period of benefit should continue at 51 weeks. Obviously, therefore, those who vote against the amendment to refer the bill back to committee for the purpose of this reconsideration are satisfied that it should stay at the figure of 36 weeks, a figure which was inserted when we were in committee of the whole. So far as we are concerned, that is not good enough.
I need not repeat the arguments which have been made. It is sufficient to say, in brief, that we feel that this is unfair action against older men who are retired, particularly in view of the abundant evidence that these men are genuinely in the labour market, which is one of the conditions upon which unemployment insurance is based.
We feel also that there is real force to the argument, since we do not know what is ahead in terms of unemployment, that it would be better to provide insurance protection during a longer period of unemployment so that benefits would be drawn as of right, rather than on any relief basis. We have protested from the beginning and shall continue to protest to the end against this reduction from 51 to 36 weeks, and I hope that even yet the government will give favourable consideration to our protests.
In addition to this retrograde step being taken by the government, we also find fault with the same government for its failure to take certain progressive steps which we feel should have been taken at this time. It is not my intention even to list all of the progressive steps that should have been taken because I wish to pinpoint the one which I feel is most important, that is the need for the extension of unemployment insurance benefits to cover periods when workers are unemployed because of illness.
We had a partial step in that direction two years ago when provision was made for the worker who has gone on unemployment insurance benefits to continue to draw his benefits even though he becomes ill, but it is still the case that a person who loses his job and becomes ill before he qualifies for benefits does not draw unemployment insurance benefits. It is also still the case that there is no provision for a worker to draw unemployment insurance benefits when he has to leave his work because of illness, no matter how many years he may have been paying into the unemployment insurance fund.
Let me make it quite clear that all of us who argue for this extension recognize that it would increase the cost; let me make it
Unemployment Insurance Act quite clear that those who speak for organized labour are ready to agree that labour should pay its share of that increased cost of this type of coverage which is long overdue in this country. As the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) pointed out, this was being argued for and sought by labour people many years ago, long before unemployment insurance came into this house. I have pleasure in reminding the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), who is in charge of the third reading of this bill, that he argued for health insurance and sickness benefits as being needed in the total picture when he spoke on the unemployment insurance bill back in 1940. Of course at that time he was just a private member.
I deeply regret that this revision of the Unemployment Insurance Act is being completed without some change to extend coverage to workers unemployed at a time of illness. I am still curious as to what consideration was given to this matter, as to how far that consideration was carried, and where it stopped. The reason I refer to consideration having been given is that we learned when we were in the committee on industrial relations that some computations had been made by the actuarial people as to what would be the additional cost of paying unemployment insurance benefits to workers laid off because of illness. It is pretty obvious to me that at some level when this revision was being considered a plan including sickness benefits was worked out, but also at some level, I suppose a higher level and maybe right at the top, that idea was killed.
I think it is most unfortunate that that happened. I am sure that many if not all members of the house agree with me that one of the lacks in this legislation, one of the lacks in our social legislation generally, is the absence of protection for the income of our working people when that income is lost because of illness. I hope that it will not be long before we will have that kind of protection, either by way of further amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act or as part of an over-all nation-wide health insurance scheme which I am sure the minister who is in charge of this third reading would like to present to the house at the earliest possible moment.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South pointed out that in the matter of unemployment more is involved than unemployment insurance. He pointed out the responsibility which rests on industry and business generally. In that same vein I would point out that when we deal with social legislation

Unemployment Insurance Act much more is required than unemployment insurance and the other bits and pieces of social legislation that we now have. We need an over-all social security program providing against unemployment; providing against loss of income due to illness; providing for health coverage; providing adequately for old age and for all other contingencies.
Once again I make an appeal to the Minister of National Health and Welfare to put up a harder fight in the cabinet for these things than apparently he has been doing lately in view of the fact that he has not brought in any new legislation for quite some time.
As both of us from this group who have spoken have indicated, we shall support the amendment before the house because we feel that the maximum period for unemployment insurance benefits should be continued at 51 weeks. We also contend that coverage of our workers when they are unemployed due to illness should be included in this legislation.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE BENEFIT RATES, ADJUST CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say only a few words in regard to the amendment before the house to refer this bill back to the committee of the whole house. The adoption of that motion would not have the effect of delaying the application of this bill in any way. There would be no need to go into the numerous details which have been discussed already while the bill has been under consideration. There were certain proposals put forward which the committee decided not to adopt in presenting this bill to the house and it is not my intention now to review those. I simply mention them to indicate that there are certain details we would wish to have included in this bill.
The present amendment deals simply with the question of the time during which benefits shall apply. The reduction to 30 weeks was proposed without any adequate supporting information. The statement that supported it was simply that it was being done in view of the high percentage of claimants who did not use the longer period. They then went on to say that it was considered justified to reduce the maximum period of entitlement to 30 weeks. The fact that it has been decided to extend it to 36 weeks is an indication that those supporting the government recognized that there was no foundation for reducing it to 30 weeks. We do submit that there is no foundation, that there is no evidence to support the reduction from 51 weeks. We want to see the 51-week period restored and that is the purpose of this amendment.

Without in any way suggesting that all the things that we would desire to see in this bill are now included in it, we do wish to emphasize that we want this bill passed; we do not want it held up. We do not want any motion that would have the effect of suspending the application of the act which will not come into effect in any event for some little time. However, we do want this longer period of benefits. Therefore I hope that hon. members on both sides of this house will support this amendment which has the declared purpose of extending the application of the act to 51 weeks.
The very fact that the government has said that there is such a high percentage that would not make claims is in itself the very best argument for retaining the 51 weeks which applied before. We submit that that argument of the government is conclusive. We submit that no statistical information has been given which would suggest any reason why this should not apply.
We have indicated over and over again that we would prefer to be discussing means by which employment can be increased rather than unemployment; nevertheless we must recognize that unemployment is a reality. We must recognize that there are many people unemployed for whom the 51 weeks is a necessary feature of this act unless there is to be hardship. We strongly urge that there be a free vote on all sides of the house to give effect to our recommendation in this respect.

maintopic: PROVISION REQUIRING LICENCE FROM GOVERNMENT OF CANADA TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN ANY IMPROVEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, while the bill is couched in general language so that it could have effect in respect of any river flowing from Canada into the United States, the main river system which has been discussed both in the house and in the standing committee on external affairs has been the Columbia river system in British Columbia and the northwestern United States. For that reason my remarks today will be centred on the Columbia river basin and the problems that have arisen in connection with it. The Columbia is of about the same importance as the St. Lawrence river system in so far as power developments are concerned. These two great rivers rank second only to the Mississippi river system on the North American continent. From that fact hon. members will realize just how important this system can be.
We were told in the standing committee that about three-fifths of the power potential of the Columbia river system is in the United States and comes entirely within the jurisdiction of our friendly neighbour. One-fifth comes under the jurisdiction of Canada alone, and the last one-fifth consists of power which can be developed in United States plants by reason of storage of water on the Columbia river system in Canada. The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources will correct me if I am wrong, but I think that is approximately the situation.
The Americans have developed their portion of the Columbia river system to a much greater extent than the Canadians. They have a great dam and plant at Grand Coulee, another large dam and plant at Bonneville, and various other power developments on the system in their territory. One result has been the establishment of a great aluminum industry in the state of Washington, another the atomic energy plant at Hanford, Washington. There has been great power development in the northwestern United States based on the Columbia river.
The Americans are now in the position where the easiest way for them to get additional power cheaply would be by storing the waters of the Columbia river and its tributaries in Canada and regulating the flow through power plants in the United States. In that way they would get greatly increased quantities of power at a very cheap rate. That is the reason the Kaiser interests were willing to build a $25 million dam in Canada at the foot of the Arrow lakes near a town by the name of Castlegar. If they had been allowed to do that they would have given the British Columbia government ownership of the dam, even though it cost $25 million,
[The Chairman.]
but of course the Kaiser companies were to get from the plants on the American side part of the power produced by the storage of this water in Canada.
