maintopic: PROVISION REQUIRING LICENCE FROM GOVERNMENT OF CANADA TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN ANY IMPROVEMENT
speechtext:
I am merely making a general introduction to my further remarks. On the Canadian side of the border there has been practically no development of the Columbia river for power purposes. There have been a few city power plants, and the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company has plants on the Kootenay river between Nelson and Castlegar. It has another large plant on the Pend d'Oreille near Waneta. The British Columbia power commission, which is a governmental body, has a power plant at What-shan on the Arrow lakes, and I believe another in east Kootenay. But there has been very little development of the Columbia river in Canada compared with the developments that have taken place in the United States. It is because of this difference that we are now faced with the fact that the Americans are very keen to have the use of the Columbia river waters in Canada for purposes of storage and regulation so they can get greatly increased amounts of power from their own plants at a very cheap rate.
When the British Columbia government announced that it had made an agreement with the Kaiser interests there was a good deal of consternation at Ottawa, for since 1944 the international joint commission had been working on a joint reference from the Canadian and United States governments

instructing them to study the potentialities of the Columbia river system in its entirety.
Down through the years the dominion officials and the British Columbia officials have worked in the closest co-operation. I can quite understand why there was annoyance here when it appeared that an agreement had been made between the British Columbia government and the Kaiser interests. Mind you, I believe there is a good deal to be said on both sides. But in any event, last fall when this agreement was announced a very bitter dispute developed between the two governments. There were harsh words used by members of the provincial government, and there were equally harsh words used by members of the dominion government. In order to stop this Kaiser deal, the dominion government introduced the bill we are now considering, Bill No. 3. At that time, it was known as the international rivers act, but I believe the committee has recommended that the name be changed to the international river improvements act which, as a matter of fact, describes the bill much more accurately than the original title.
The party to which I have the honour to belong, the Conservative party, took the position during the debate on the resolution preceding this bill and on second reading that we would reserve our right to take a stand for or against the bill until after it had been considered by a committee. We urged, and I think we were the first ones to do so, that this bill be sent to a standing committee for study. We had in mind the wisdom of hearing evidence from both the dominion and provincial officials, and also of giving the people of British Columbia an opportunity to learn from the press and over the radio what the dispute was about. Even more particularly, we had in mind that if the Columbia river system in Canada was to be developed that could only be achieved by co-operation between the two governments. It was quite obvious that this development would never take place unless the two governments started once again to co-operate as they had been doing until this Kaiser deal came into the picture.
Eventually our suggestion was accepted and the bill went to the standing committee on external affairs. The committee had many meetings, and it heard many witnesses. Today I should like to pay tribute, in the first place, to the chairman of that committee, the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Picard). He and I do not always agree, but I thought he conducted the affairs of that committee in an excellent way. A great deal of the credit for the success which the committee has achieved must go to him. Then, too, I should like to pay tribute to the members from other parts
International Rivers
of Canada who sat on that committee. Here they were, hearing evidence day after day at great length about a river system in British Columbia of which they knew nothing. Many of them had never been west of Toronto. Perhaps I should not say that; perhaps I should say Winnipeg. In any event, it must have been very difficult for them to follow the evidence. However, they stuck with the committee throughout and they deserve great credit for the manner in which they considered this bill.
There were several amendments made in the committee and today I propose to refer briefly to four of them. One of these amendments was made to section 7, and that amendment took out of the operation of the act irrigation systems and improvements in those rivers which were designed for domestic or sanitary purposes. It would have been unthinkable in British Columbia to have the irrigation systems in the Columbia river and its tributaries under licence control from the dominion. It would have been intolerable.
I think it would almost have been grounds for civil war in that part of Canada! In any event, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Lesage) saw the objection and clause 7, paragraph (c), has been recommended to the house. It has the effect of exempting improvements of that kind from the operation of the bill.
There was also a clause written into the bill making it clear that provincial laws would apply to these international river systems except where such laws were repugnant to this particular bill. This is now clause 10 of the bill and it reads as follows:
Notwithstanding anything in this act an international river improvement shall be subject to the same laws to which it would be subject il it were a river improvement within the legislative jurisdiction of the legislature of the province in which it is situated except in so far as such provincial laws are repugnant to this act or the regulations.
That was a beneficial amendment. Then, in the new clause 11 there was a further amendment providing for an annual report to parliament. This change also was all to the good. There were several other minor amendments, but the fourth amendment to which I shall refer today was the deletion from the bill of what was originally clause 9. Clause 9 read as follows:
All international river improvements heretofore or hereafter constructed, and not excepted from the operation of this act, are hereby declared to be works for the general advantage of Canada.
That was the clause that upset the British Columbia government more than any other part of the act. They argued, and I think correctly, if that clause remained in the bill it had the effect of nationalizing the two

International Rivers
main drainage basins in British Columbia. In the first place, it affected the Columbia river system which takes up the whole southeastern part of the province, and in the second place the territory in northwestern British Columbia which is drained by great rivers like the Taku and Stikine and some others which flow through the panhandle of Alaska. Because they happen to flow for a few miles in Alaska before they reach the sea, they become subject to the terms of this bill. I read from page 19 of the British Columbia government brief where they deal with this point in the following words:
In effect, this bill and what may be done under it is wide enough to nationalize the two major drainage basins of the province of British Columbia, and far from being a measure providing for control by negation it is, in the opinion of the government of British Columbia, a bill by which the national government without provincial consent is enabled to develop and utilize certain of the water resources of our province . . .
The main argument in the committee between dominion and provincial government officials had to do with the effects of leaving this clause 9 in the act. Fortunately, in the final analysis, the dominion agreed to drop that clause and I hope thereby paved the way for full co-operation between the dominion and the province of British Columbia in the development of this Columbia river system now and, in a few years' time, the systems of rivers which flow through the panhandle of Alaska.
At this time I suggest to the government that it be very careful about using this power to declare works of any kind as being works for the general advantage of Canada. It seems to me that the fathers of confederation never intended that the dominion government should use that particular provision of the British North America Act to take over a whole group of improvements in any part of Canada. I think they meant to have it there as a reserve power to be used very sparingly where some particular work was obviously for the general advantage of Canada.
The provision is contained in section 92 of the British North America Act, which gives the provinces their exclusive powers. That section reads:
In each province the legislature may exclusively make laws in relation to matters coming within the classes of subjects next hereinafter enumerated.
Then the section goes on to enumerate a number of subjects, one of which is as follows:
10. Local works and undertakings other than such as are of the following classes-

And then we come to the type of work lifted out of the provisions of section 92. Subsection 10(c) is as follows:
Such works as, although wholly situate within the province, are before or after their execution declared by the parliament of Canada to be for the general advantage of Canada or for the advantage of two or more of the provinces.
It is obvious that in the case of this bill the dominion deliberately inserted clause 9 to make sure that if it did not have jurisdiction otherwise, because the water flowed over the border, it would in any event have power by using this declaration. I think it was a mistake to do that; and I am glad the minister saw fit to consent to the deletion of that clause from the bill.
That is a rough sketch of the changes made in the bill when it was before the standing committee on external affairs. Now that these changes have been made-and I presume they will be accepted by the house-the Conservative party is glad to support the bill. We realize some amendments may be suggested while the bill is in committee of the whole, and of course we would want to feel free to consider any such amendments. But as it stands at the present time we are prepared to support it.
However, we would repeat the warning we gave in the earlier stages of the debate, namely that there must be co-operation between the two governments if this Columbia river system is to be developed adequately. Bill No. 3 gives the dominion licensing control over all the works on any one of these river systems which affect the flow of water over the border. That is a very wide control. To a degree the dominion is stepping in and taking control over the improvements on these rivers. Yet at the same time it appears to be expecting somebody else to put up the money to build such improvements.
I suggest that is a weak position.
It is true that the dominion has spent several million dollars on surveys of the Columbia river system; but essentially the picture today is that the dominion government will be able to say, "You cannot erect an improvement on this international river" -or some other international river. Yet it is not going to put up any of the money to help build that improvement. I think that policy must be changed. The time has come when the dominion government must either contribute to the construction of some of these river improvements or, at the very least, place its credit behind the provincial government that is proposing to go ahead with the development. The dominion can raise money at much lower rates than any of the provinces, with the exception of

Ontario and Quebec. I believe the time has come in Canada when we must have a joint investment policy for the development of these great resources. These are developments which are in the nature of public utilities, and the dominion should be ready to place its credit behind some of these developments.

maintopic: PROVISION REQUIRING LICENCE FROM GOVERNMENT OF CANADA TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN ANY IMPROVEMENT
speechtext: We want that on the Saint John river, too.

maintopic: PROVISION REQUIRING LICENCE FROM GOVERNMENT OF CANADA TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN ANY IMPROVEMENT
speechtext:
Yes, the Saint John river development is another very good example of a case where there must be help from the dominion. At the meeting of the premiers held here in April that was one of the subjects agreed upon for discussion at the forthcoming meeting this fall. It was described as public investments and natural resources development. The Conservative party feels the time has come when there must be a joint investment program adopted by the dominion.
The dominion must take one other step. It must negotiate quickly with the United States government for a treaty covering downstream benefits. It is obvious that there is going to be water stored in the Canadian part of the Columbia river system. It is also obvious that that water will increase the production of power in United States plants. The very fact that the water is stored and regulated means that the Americans can develop more power, because it means that at low water there will be more water flowing through their plants than there has been in the past.
We believe that the dominion must move at once to negotiate a treaty covering downstream benefits. General McNaughton dealt with that in his evidence before the committee, when he said this:
In order to protect the interests of Canada in the case of the construction of reservoirs in Canada which benefit projects downstream in the United States it will be necessary therefore, in advance of construction, to enter into a treaty or agreement precisely defining the amount and form of recompense to Canada for the natural resources of Canada contributed to the project.
The minister himself said something to the same effect when he spoke in the house about a month ago. I believe it cannot be questioned that there must be a treaty negotiated with the United States. I have before me the report of a statement made by the minister, as it appears in the press of May 21. Premier Bennett of British Columbia had suggested a summit conference between the governments of the United States, Canada and British Columbia. The Minister of
International Rivers
Northern Affairs and National Resources made a statement in reply, and the newspaper article is as follows:
"Summit conferences must be preceded by detailed studies", Lesage said. "It will be better to continue discussions between these two groups of experts and try to work out either a formula, or else to lay down principles on downstream benefits. We might then have high level talks when we have reached some degree of agreement."
The federal minister said he had emphasized in his recent Vancouver speech that the first requirement for international co-operation in the Columbia is American agreement to the principle that Canada must share in downstream benefits accruing to the United States through development in Canada.
Unfortunately time is running out for the negotiation of a treaty of that kind. We were warned of that by General McNaughton in the committee. One of the particular developments in British Columbia is ready to be gone ahead with and I refer to the Mica creek project. This involves the construction of a huge dam about 100 miles north of Revelstoke on the main line right at the top of the bend of the Columbia river. It is estimated that that dam and power plant will cost about $245 million. General McNaughton agreed that it could be proceeded with right away, and the British Columbia government is also in agreement that the project should go ahead. The Americans are anxious to do it; the Americans are sitting there now with the money ready to build that dam and power plant. All they want is the word to go ahead.
Some of us feel that if we invite the Americans into our country to build that project, even though they say it will become the property of the British Columbia government, we should make no mistake about it, if they build that project they are going to have a great deal to say about what is to be done with the power. Canada will be put in an impossible position if it allows that situation to develop.
We had placed before us reports which had been submitted to the Americans in connection with various developments that could take place on the Columbia river. One of them was to the effect that the Mica creek project could be developed by a group of utility companies in the United States known as the Puget Sound utilities council, which consists of the following five utility organizations: Seattle City Light, Tacoma City Light, Puget Sound Power and Light Company, Snohomish county public utility district No. 1, Chelan county public utility district No. 1. They are quite prepared to put up the money to build this Mica creek project.
Mind you, they will be able to do that because they will have behind them the

International Rivers
credit of the United States federal government. This project is ten times the size of the Kaiser dam project which would cost only $25 million. If this plan is gone ahead with we will have United States federal government money building the Mica creek dam and power plant. This report contains some other significant statements as follows:
The Mica creek dam on the upper Columbia river in British Columbia, proposed for joint construction by council utilities, is by far the most significant storage development possible in the northwest. It would impound 10*5 million acre feet of usable storage for power production in British Columbia and the United States. Furthermore, this project is unusual in that it has a minimum of conflict with other interests. Some road relocation would be required but no conflict would be created with local economies such as large towns, farming communities or other important domestic improvements. There would be no railroad relocation, nor any problem of anadromous fish passage. This reach of the river is not navigable.
Then there is this further paragraph:
The Puget Sound utilities council has discussed the following proposal with representatives of Canada as one possibility, among others, that might be considered.
(1) Council utilities, at their own expense, would construct a dam on the Columbia river near the mouth of Mica creek at the estimated cost of $250,000,000. Although the council would finance the project, the province of British Columbia would own it.
The premier of British Columbia has been negotiating with these people even since the meetings of the standing committee on external affairs. In the committee I asked the attorney general whether it was the policy of the British Columbia government to have the Americans develop the Mica creek project. The questions and answers begin at page 347 of the proceedings but I shall not bother to read the introductory comments. At the top of page 348 I am reported as asking the attorney general:
Is your government adopting a policy of that kind?
I was referring to having the Americans come in and build the Mica creek project.

maintopic: PROVISION REQUIRING LICENCE FROM GOVERNMENT OF CANADA TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN ANY IMPROVEMENT
speechtext:
No, I would say that there is no policy of that kind by the government of British Columbia.
We have seen press dispatches reporting that the Puget Sound utilities council representatives have been in Victoria discussing this question with the premier, with Mr. Sommers, minister of lands, and Mr. Bonner since the meetings of the committee. On May 3 the premier of British Columbia is reported as follows:
The premier added that federal government interference on the Kaiser dam proposals at Arrow lakes had prevented the B.C. government from entering similar arrangements for the building of a big dam at Mica creek.
fMr. Green.]
The cost of the Mica creek project has been estimated as high as $275,000,000.
"The Kaiser dam was only a part of the project," the premier said. "These dams would be built without cost to us and we would get the cheapest power in the world."
Do you mean," he was asked, "that the same American financing arrangement would have been used on the Mica creek development?"
Certainly," he said, "and it has been delayed by the federal government.
The situation is that we Conservatives believe that that project should be built by Canada, by the dominion and the British Columbia governments working together. We advocate the adoption at once of a joint investment policy for projects of this kind. It might be that a Columbia river authority could be set up to do this work with the financial credit of the dominion and the province behind it, but that is a matter of detail. The main point is that Canadians must undertake this work.
In the final analysis there is going to be about one billion dollars spent on the development of the Columbia river system in Canada. This is one of the biggest developments in our whole nation, too big and too important to be handled by those outside the country. This is a great opportunity to strengthen this nation and we believe it can be done by co-operation between the two governments.
Finally we would like to emphasize again the need for a national energy policy and the setting up of a national energy board in Ottawa or some governmental authority of that type. One reason why this dispute arose between the dominion and the British Columbia governments was that here in Ottawa there were half a dozen different groups of people dealing with this question. We had General McNaughton and the international joint commission, and this matter was rather far removed from their regular job. General McNaughton took the initiative in this matter and if it had not been for him I hate to think what the position would be at the present time.
I have nothing but praise for the conduct of General McNaughton in his actions in connection with this problem. We had the international joint commission as one body here dealing with this question. Then we had and still have the minister's water branch in the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. We have the Department of Trade and Commerce. Of course, they are in everything under the present minister. We need expect nothing else than to have their finger in every pie around Ottawa, and they were in this pie as well. The economic adviser for all these projects is Dr. John Davis of the Department of Trade

and Commerce. Then for pipe lines we have the Department of Transport, which has no experts at all to deal with such questions. Then we have the board of transport commissioners with some jurisdiction also in regard to oil and gas pipe lines.
Here in Ottawa there is confusion in the directing of efforts to settle this problem. We believe Canada will never have a national energy policy, will never have a proper policy for the development of these sources of energy, until we have a national energy board. I made this argument on February 25, and I have no intention of going into it in any greater detail at the present time, but I merely sum it up by saying this. Water power, oil, gas, uranium and coal are the five great sources of energy in this country. Canada is fortunate in having all five of them. They will make this nation one of the great nations of the world if good leadership is given here in Ottawa. Once again we urge upon the dominion government that it take steps at once to set up a national energy board for the purpose of studying these various questions and formulating a national energy policy and of having a group of trained men who could implement the policy once it had been adopted by the government.

maintopic: PROVISION REQUIRING LICENCE FROM GOVERNMENT OF CANADA TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN ANY IMPROVEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is a very important measure occasioned by the need to ensure the sound and satisfactory development of international rivers in Canada. The rapidly increasing demand for power and the publicity surrounding the terms of this legislation have almost overnight caused many Canadians to realize the great and increasing value of our water resources and the need for this type of legislation to protect them, in so far as international rivers are concerned.
As the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra said, the discussions in the previous debates and in the committee centred very largely in the proposed developments of the Columbia river, and naturally so on account of the proposals by the provincial government at that time to permit the Kaiser Corporation to build a dam at the lower Arrow lakes. Now, this legislation is of particular concern to my constituents because they all happen to live in the Columbia river basin, as do the constituents of the hon. members for Kootenay East, Okanagan Boundary and Okanagan-Revelstoke. On that account I have received a large number of resolutions and briefs and hundreds of letters from individuals. I have received resolutions and briefs from municipalities, trade unions, farmers' institutes, women's institutes, chambers of commerce, engineering groups and, as I said before, a large number of individuals, who passed these resolutions and wrote these briefs and sent
International Rivers
letters to me because they were very seriously concerned about this whole matter and interested in developments with respect to this legislation.
Many of my constituents have followed very closely the proceedings in this house in connection with the bill and the proceedings in the committee on external affairs when this measure was being discussed. I must say that the work of the committee on external affairs was in my opinion unusually interesting, owing to the importance of the bill and the evidence presented by various witnesses and the focusing of the attention of the committee on the proposed developments in the Columbia river basin. To the people of my constituency, as I said before, it was especially interesting because of its relation to the proposal for the building of a dam on the lower Arrow Lakes.
I must, in fairness, like the previous speaker, congratulate the chairman of the committee on the very fair and efficient performance of his duties under circumstances which at times required quite a high degree of tact, fairness and the consideration of various points of view. There is no question about it that certain members of the committee had very strong views with respect to this legislation and its application. The chairman's arrangements for procedure, the agenda, and the hearing of evidence were very fair, in my opinion, to all parties concerned. Personally I think the chairman is to be congratulated on the way in which he carried out the expressed wishes of the committee in seeing that all provincial governments were notified of the meetings of the committee and that they had the opportunity to make representations.
The first witness to appear before the committee was General McNaughton whose knowledge and grasp of the problems relating to the development of international rivers greatly impressed the members of the committee. There is no question about that. Without a doubt, General McNaughton will be recognized in Canadian history as the architect of the draft plans for the wise development of the Columbia and other international rivers, and the prime and first advocate of the principle of downstream benefits in Canada. The committee recognized this in its report, and I think I should place on record part of that report:
Your committee was favourably impressed by the work performed to date by the chairman, members and officials of the Canadian section of the international joint commission concerning the elaboration of projects for the over-all development and maximum use of hydro-electric power to be derived from the Columbia river basin and the possible use of the Kootenay and Fraser rivers in relation thereto.

International Rivers
Your committee also approves of the stand taken by the chairman of the Canadian section of the international joint commission for the protection of Canadian interests, in its dealings with the members of the U.S. section of the commission.
The members of this house and Canadians generally owe a debt of gratitude to General McNaughton for the way he has applied himself to the great river development problems that are facing Canada at the present time and for his vigorous defence of Canadian interests and Canadian rights on all occasions.
The committee also heard Mr. Varcoe, the deputy minister of justice, on the constitutional aspects of the bill, and Mr. M. H. Wershof, of the Department of External Affairs, on international law in relation to the bill. I think it is fair to say that the committee gained a great deal of valuable information from both these witnesses.
Then the committee heard the Hon. R. W. Bonner, attorney general of British Columbia, who presented the brief for his province. Whatever our opinions concerning the views presented, it must be admitted by members of the committee that Mr. Bonner was a skilful witness who presented his government's case to the best possible advantage, particularly his government's objection to clause 9 in the bill as sent to the committee originally. I can well appreciate that objection. According to my understanding of Mr. Bonner's evidence, it was possibly the major objection that his government had to the bill and did create certain fears in the minds of the members of his government.
As I said before, the committee made arrangements for all provinces to be notified that representations would be heard by the committee if they saw fit to attend. There were representations from only two provinces. In the first case the minister of agriculture in the government of Saskatchewan, while he agreed with the principle of the bill, was concerned as to whether the intention of the Canadian government to insist that a licence be obtained under this act applied to the thousands of small domestic and irrigation projects built and to be built for farmers on the prairies, and suggested that the bill be amended to clarify this section. In response to that request the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources proposed an amendment which was recommended by the committee and which was satisfactory to the minister of agriculture for the province of Saskatchewan.
Then Mr. Bonner, on behalf of the government of British Columbia, took particular exception to clause 9 of the bill which, as I said before, made it possible to declare
[Mr. Herridge.l
all international river improvements not exempted from the operation of the act works for the general advantage of Canada. I could well appreciate the fears and the concern over this section. It is a very strong section. After careful consideration of Mr. Bonner's representations the minister recommended to the committee deletion of this clause from the bill. I think the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources is to be commended for his spirit of compromise and his willingness to meet the legitimate fears of any province concerned. I think in the two cases where amendments arose as to this matter, he showed a spirit of compromise and a willingness to do what he could to meet these fears and yet at the same time not affect the protection of the national interest in these international rivers.
After the minister had proposed his last amendment, he was congratulated by members of all parties in the committee on his consideration of representations made for amendments to the bill and on his willingness, as I said before, to allay the fears which certain sections of the bill created in the minds of the representatives of the provincial governments concerned.
At this stage I think I should say that the evidence given by the officials of the water resources branch of his department was of great assistance to the committee. I think these officials should be particularly mentioned because, as a matter of fact, all the mass of data that we had the opportunity to deal with, including all the engineering data placed before the committee, is entirely the result of the work and the technical experience of the engineers of the water resources branch of the minister's department and the engineers of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys and the Department of Public Works. I think the evidence indicated that there has been going on for the last ten years a thorough and complete survey of the Columbia river basin.
Mr. Chairman, we consider that this bill lays the foundation for the development of international rivers in Canada as the result of federal-provincial co-operation which we hope to see develop in the future. The people of British Columbia, particularly the residents of my constituency, are, as the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra said, greatly interested in seeing the development of the great projects, such as the Mica creek dam, that have been mentioned during this discussion.
Speaking in this house as far back as February 22, 1949 on behalf of this group and presenting the policy and views of this group

in respect of this matter, I urged the establishment of a Columbia river basin authority. I am going to do something that I think the late Hon. Ian Mackenzie did on one occasion; I am going to quote myself. I am going to read from Hansard of February 22, 1949, page 775.

My second suggestion is that consideration should be given by this government to the development of the water resources in the basin under public ownership in co-operation with the government of British Columbia. I am recommending the establishment of a Canadian Columbia river basin authority, and in support of that proposal I should like to quote from the minutes of a committee of congress which sat in 1933-34 to consider this question and which reported with respect to the United States portion of the Columbia river basin as follows:
This is an extremely interesting quotation from a committee report in the United States dealing with the development of the Columbia river basin in the United States.
"We believe in private enterprise-in the expectancy of rewards for honest endeavour, labour, initiative and daring-in the things that have made America great. But some things are too big for private enterprise, and the Columbia river is one of these."

To my knowledge, Mr. Chairman, this was the first suggestion made in the House of Commons for the establishment of such an authority and it captured the imagination of large numbers of people in British Columbia. maintopic: PROVISION REQUIRING LICENCE FROM GOVERNMENT OF CANADA TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN ANY IMPROVEMENT
speechtext:
There is overwhelming
evidence to prove the value of public power development, and 1 want to conclude on that note. I was noticing recently that, according to the Tennessee valley authority director of information in the United States, $429 million of the taxpayers' money was invested in the Morse-Hell's canyon-plan, the government borrowing at about 21 per cent.
Over the past 21 years of operation the margin has amounted to an average of 4 per cent return on the net average power investment, which is about double the cost of money to the government during that period.
What an excellent example that is for our federal and provincial governments to follow; I refer to the example of the Tennessee valley authority.
According to testimony by this same gentleman, there was a 200 per cent increase in local industry as the result of the development of the Tennessee valley authority as against the meagre 75 per cent increase in industry in New England under free enterprise control of power in the same period of time. After the Tennessee valley authority was established, 1,600 new, privately owned industries were set up in a region where private industry electrical experts testified previously no progress could be made with power development. The result of the Tennessee valley authority development was a 500 per cent increase in per capita income in the region, flood control, forestry and agricultural aid, and general economic improvement.

International Rivers
The success of the Ontario hydro commission demonstrates what can be done with respect to these public power projects. It has meant a great deal to industry and agriculture in Ontario. As the result of its public power policy the government of Saskatchewan is now electrifying the majority of the farms in that province, farms that would have remained without light and power if they had been left to the mercy of private power developments. In addition, the British Columbia power commission, established under the coalition government of Premier Hart, has brought power to thousands of people in the interior of British Columbia who would be without power and electric light today if it had not been provided by the publicly owned power facilities of the British Columbia power commission. What an opportunity the Columbia river developments provide for the British Columbia power commission, working in co-operation with the federal government.
However, Mr. Chairman, in Canada and the United States the opponents of public power development continue to be active. In this connection I want to quote very briefly from the remarks of former President Truman when speaking at Portland on the Pacific coast last week. Unfortunately, under the present Republican government of the United States there is a great tendency to revert to private power development and to undermine the good work of public power development on the Columbia, in the Tennessee valley, on the Missouri and other rivers.
Former President Truman was speaking in this connection at Portland and was dealing with the Columbia at that time. I will say that former President Truman, as was former President Roosevelt, was always a strong advocate of public power development in the United States. I was interested in this article because it indicates what is happening south of the line in the Columbia river basin and what might have happened in Canada and could happen if some people had their way. The article reads:
In his prepared speech Mr. Truman asserted that "selfish interests" with public lands and public power as their targets had been "more subtle and, for that reason, more dangerous" during the last two years.
"Pious in his pretensions and aided by experts in propaganda", the former president said, "the modern day raider insists he is fighting for private enterprise, local rights, regional rights and state rights. But he always winds up by taking over the people's rights."
The former president charged that during this period "there has been an attempt to becloud the basic concept that our great rivers are a federal responsibility."
"A number of people," he went on. "have been trying to make us believe that the federal interest

in our river systems is an encroachment on the rights of the states and local governments."
We have heard that sort of talk in this country.
"There have been a lot of crocodile tears about how the federal government is setting up a power monopoly and breaking down states rights-and how the time has come to get the federal government out of the river business. The development of our rivers must be planned-it cannot be opened as a grab bag to private interests to pick off the best revenue-producing dam sites at the expense of future generations." . . .
Of the methods of the "raiders" he said further that "if you have an agency like the southwestern power administration, selling power at a low cost to rural co-operatives, the technique is to rewrite the contracts in such a way that the co-operatives will have to go out of business."
Or, he went on, "if you have a new source of publicly-financed power coming into being, like the St. Lawrence project, they try to give the power to the private companies to distribute without any guarantees in the public interest. If you have a great plan for an entire river basin, like the plan for the Columbia, which is only partly built", he said, "then the technique is for the federal government to give up the crucial dam sites and get the federal power commission to turn them over to private power companies for piecemeal exploitation. This will block the future growth of the whole system and prevent existing dams from turning out as much power as they could."
When this bill is adopted by the house it will prevent that sort of thing happening in Canada, and will ensure the sound development of our international rivers in the national interest.
Finally, I want to bring to the attention of the committee again that the Columbia river basin is rich in natural resources. There is an abundance of land, forest and mineral wealth which provides great opportunities for industrial and agricultural development if we harness the water resources of the region. Experience has proven this can best be done under public ownership, and to the great advantage of the public in general.
Therefore to this end, on behalf of this group I again strongly urge the establishment of a Columbia river basin authority, after the fashion of the successful Tennessee valley authority, and a program of public investment as the result of federal-provincial co-operation that will provide power for the development of our natural resources and also provide, as the years go by, the flood protection so necessary on many parts of this river. The party I have the honour to represent advocates the development of Canadian natural resources for Canadians first, and believes the bill provides a sound foundation for the development of international rivers in Canada to the advantage of this dominion. We trust that, on the sound foundations laid by the bill, there will be erected an enduring

structure of federal-provincial co-operation in the future development of our international rivers.

maintopic: PROVISION REQUIRING LICENCE FROM GOVERNMENT OF CANADA TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN ANY IMPROVEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in rising to say a few words on the bill before us, may I first of all say that I agree with the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources in his words of congratulation to the committee for the splendid work done during the many sessions when the bill was under study and consideration. We appreciate many of the changes that have been made, especially the deletion of clause 9 and the excepting from the regulations of the various irrigation projects in the interior and elsewhere in British Columbia.
I am not going to deal with the measure at great length. I have spoken about it on previous occasions. I expressed what I thought then, and I am going to tell you I have had no reason to regret any statement I ever made during those speeches. I still feel with regard to the bill as I did on those former occasions, although it has been modified to a considerable degree.
I was particularly pleased in reading the reports of the proceedings of the committee to note that the minister expressed a real feeling of co-operation. We hope that will continue, because we know it is necessary in order to develop the many projects representing about 50 per cent of the potential power of British Columbia covered by the bill. I was also impressed by the fact that the evidence presented before the committee proved that many of the claims made by those supporting the bill in the earlier debate were irresponsible and ill-founded. However, that is all in the past. As I said, I am not going into that further.
The federal government is determined to carry on with its plan to impose its authority, and like all good Canadians living in the province of British Columbia I shall abide by the law. However, I have a few points I should like to bring to the attention of the minister, and possibly certain questions to ask. I would ask that they be clarified, perhaps not individually as they are brought ap but some time before this debate is concluded. I shall try to be brief and concise in presenting these questions, so the minister will have no difficulty in discerning what I am trying to get at and in formulating his answers.
First, what will be the status of British Columbia licences in so far as international rivers are concerned? Is it planned that the licence fees for federal licences under this bill shall be only nominal? I expect the
International Rivers
minister is going to say, read clause 10. I have read clause 10, Mr. Chairman, and the first part of it is wonderful. In fact when I first read it I said that was in effect a cancellation of this whole bill. Then I saw the words, "except in so far as such provincial laws are repugnant to this act or the regulations." Those words could be interpreted rather widely. There could be regulations made under this act which would make any act of the province of British Columbia repugnant to it.
In that connection, is it intended to make regulations that will be at variance with the British Columbia water rights legislation, and so destroy it? Another thing about which I should like clarification is the status of the projects in operation. I can refer to three of which I know at the moment. There is the Whatshan project and the Spilli-macheen; those are both British Columbia power installations. Then we have the large Consolidated Mining and Smelting installation which I believe is known as the Corra Linn dam. Will these projects be automatically licensed? It seems rather unusual to have legislation of this kind made retroactive, and I am wondering what the answer will be in this case.
We have heard something about downstream benefits, Mr. Chairman, and this is a very important question. It is the problem which is presented as the reason for introducing this Bill No. 3. I admit it is a very important problem; but if it is going to be the basis on which the whole development of the Columbia is to take place is it not fitting that it should be the first problem upon which all parties concerned are satisfied? The parties concerned are, of course, the province of British Columbia, the government of Canada and the government or official representative of the United States of America.
Recently I was glad to see that the premier of British Columbia had called for a top level conference to discuss this matter. Immediately our own minister in charge of this department made a reply by way of the press. He said he did not think that was the right way to go about it, that the idea was premature. I referred to the splendid spirit of co-operation which had been evidenced by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. I am beginning to wonder if this long distance fight is still going to be carried on via the press of this country.
Speaking of downstream benefits, I have heard it said that this principle has never been recognized by the United States. I think

International Rivers
that is an incorrect statement. I believe we should give credit to the British Columbia government for gaining the first recognition of the value of downstream benefits in their dealings over the Kaiser dam, which I had not intended to mention. In the proposed contract the United States recognized that such a thing as downstream benefits existed, and they were prepared to pay British Columbia for what they were receiving by way of increased power. Whether or not these payments were in accordance with actual value I am not going to argue at the moment. But I am going to say that the British Columbia government established for Canada and for the international joint commission the right of Canada or the right of any province to downstream benefits in the United States.
As a further argument that this conference should be held at once, I am going to refer for a moment to the matter of Mica creek. Mica creek is a very important project to the people of the interior of British Columbia. We would like to see it started at the earliest possible moment. No one in this house can say that if and when that dam is built the United States will not receive the same downstream benefits they would have received had the proposed Kaiser dam been put into operation. If we intend to get speedy action on the Mica creek dam, as I hope we will, then we must have speedy action at this top level conference of the three parties most vitally concerned in order to consider the whole problem of downstream benefits. We have heard also of co-operative plans for the development of the Columbia basin. I am pleased to say that the hon. member for Kootenay West is the father of that idea, and I will give him credit for it. In connection with that development, Mr. Chairman, I am going to suggest that we have a top level board, and by top level I mean government representatives of the two parties most vitally concerned, the government of Canada and the government of British Columbia.
At the moment surveys are being made and some plans are being formulated, but it is not being done at the top level. It is being done by what I would call junior engineers and junior assistants. We have been told that there are groups with all kinds of money at their beck and call awaiting the development of the Columbia basin. Whether or not that is going ahead in the near future, of course, is more or less conjecture; but I am confident that the government of British Columbia did have plans whereby this great Columbia basin would be developed in the near future. If we are now going to have something which will slow up that development, and throw a monkey wrench, if you 
will, into the private development of this great basin, then I am going to suggest that we have immediate action by the government of Canada in announcing a program to replace the program which the province had planned. I do not think that is an unreasonable request. I believe that where any plan or any project is stopped, it is up to those responsible for the stoppage of that program or project to bring in an alternative.
These are the points I wanted to outline. I am sure the minister will be able to clarify these various matters that bother me and, perhaps, bother a great many other people in Canada. The attitude of the government should be made known at once so the uncertainty in the minds of people in British Columbia and throughout Canada may be put at rest.

maintopic: PROVISION REQUIRING LICENCE FROM GOVERNMENT OF CANADA TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN ANY IMPROVEMENT

maintopic: PROVISION REQUIRING LICENCE FROM GOVERNMENT OF CANADA TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN ANY IMPROVEMENT
speechtext:

mean that he wants the Canadian members of the commission to discuss it among themselves and then recommend to the Canadian government what the Canadian government should do?

speechtext: I mean a discussion in the international joint commission between the Canadian members and the United States members, in order to see if it will be possible to find a general formula which will be applicable on both sides of the border and all along the border for downstream benefits; and if it is not possible to find a definite formula, establish at least a set of principles, in order of priority, from which a formula could be devised in each case which would be workable.

maintopic: PROVISION REQUIRING LICENCE FROM GOVERNMENT OF CANADA TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN ANY IMPROVEMENT

maintopic: PROVISION REQUIRING LICENCE FROM GOVERNMENT OF CANADA TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN ANY IMPROVEMENT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I had not intended to take any part in this debate, but as the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has so obviously missed the point I think it is well to point out one or two things.

maintopic: PROVISION REQUIRING LICENCE FROM GOVERNMENT OF CANADA TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN ANY IMPROVEMENT
speechtext: Be sure you set me straight. I shall be glad to hear it.

maintopic: PROVISION REQUIRING LICENCE FROM GOVERNMENT OF CANADA TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN ANY IMPROVEMENT
speechtext:
The hon. member read a section of the minutes in which General McNaughton said we could proceed with the Mica creek project but that timing was of the essence, shall we say. Those are not his exact words. I am not quoting; I am simply paraphrasing. When he said that I think he showed, without putting it into words, the value of the over-all survey, and more particularly the survey on which we are this year spending some $260,000; that is the survey to determine whether the Columbia may be diverted economically and feasibly into the Fraser river system for development of that water here in Canada.
For some time discussions have been going on in the international joint commission as to downstream benefits, and whether Canada may expect to receive benefits for water stored on our territory. When General McNaughton made his presentation before the committee he showed quite conclusively that we may store sufficient water in Canada.

to double the power output of the Columbia system in the United States. That is a tremendous amount of power, and it is certainly of tremendous value to the American people.
As recently as April 5, 1955, the international joint commission met, I note from the minutes, in open meeting in Washington. At that time General McNaughton gave almost the identical summary of the project of the whole development of the Columbia basin to the international joint commission over which Mr. Len Jordan-I believe he is Governor Len Jordan-was presiding. After hearing all of the evidence Mr. Jordan summed up General McNaughton's interpretation of the value of the water stored and the possible value of the storage for downstream benefits. I should just like to quote in order to show that Len Jordan has missed the point by almost as wide a margin as has the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. Summing up, Len Jordan said this:
And, also-if I am wrong, I hope you will correct me-it seemed to me that you ascribed some new value to storage which I am not able to see.
I agree that regulating the flow, the flood flows of a river, has certain beneficial effects. I will point out, though, that the mere act of storing water does not increase the quantity of that water. Nothing new has been added.
Then this is the crowning achievement of the statement:
As a matter of fact, by the very storing of the water you lose by the depletion occasioned by evaporation.
If that is the value put by the United States section of the international joint commission on the 16 million acre feet of water we may store in Canada for regulated flow into the United States turbines, then I say it is quite essential that we have some firm understanding as to how we may develop our water resources here in Canada before we go into negotiations with United States authorities to determine what downstream benefits they are prepared to pay.

Certainly if that course is followed there will be further trouble between the dominion

maintopic: PROVISION REQUIRING LICENCE FROM GOVERNMENT OF CANADA TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN ANY IMPROVEMENT
speechtext: I am sure the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has enough imagination to guess how agreements with other countries are arrived at. First of all we have to sound out the opinion in the other country. We have to know if an agreement is possible. Then, after we know if an agreement is possible, we have to discuss with them the form the agreement will take. The best way of learning whether an agreement is possible on the question of downstream benefits is for the Canadian members of the international joint commission to ascertain the opinion of the United States members and see if it is possible to arrive at some kind of formula or, in the absence of a formula, some kind of principles that can be laid down. After we have the answer to that it will then be possible to sound out the United States government in order to know in what form the agreement should be written. It seems to me that is logical, and I cannot go any further.

maintopic: PROVISION REQUIRING LICENCE FROM GOVERNMENT OF CANADA TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN ANY IMPROVEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in taking part in the deliberations of the committee this afternoon may I say I have noticed there have been quite a number of expressions of appreciation to various individuals and groups, and first of all I should like to join in those words of appreciation. The government has shown a willingness to accept certain amendments which, I suggest, make the bill in many respects a much different bill from the one originally presented to us. Comparing the one originally presented to us with the present bill we can readily see that substantial changes have been made.
I am sure all members of the committee who have taken even a cursory glance at the proceedings of the standing committee on external affairs will be well aware of the fact that the measure received careful and diligent study in that committee.
On the one hand there were those who felt that the measure was essential to the proper development of resources in the national interest. On the other hand there were those who were convinced that it was not only unnecessary but was a violation of the rights of the provinces in respect to these matters. Although I fully appreciate the position in which the chairman found himself as he

endeavoured to maintain peace and order, I must say there were times when he, as chairman, was inclined to be overly loquacious, and there were times when I would say he evidenced rather a political bias.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: PROVISION REQUIRING LICENCE FROM GOVERNMENT OF CANADA TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN ANY IMPROVEMENT
speechtext: Order. Perhaps the hon. member will not mind my enlarging on that by pointing out that if that were not the case we might have grave difficulty in ever getting anybody to assume the responsibilities involved in the chairmanship of a committee.

maintopic: PROVISION REQUIRING LICENCE FROM GOVERNMENT OF CANADA TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN ANY IMPROVEMENT

maintopic: PROVISION REQUIRING LICENCE FROM GOVERNMENT OF CANADA TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN ANY IMPROVEMENT

maintopic: PROVISION REQUIRING LICENCE FROM GOVERNMENT OF CANADA TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN ANY IMPROVEMENT

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: PROVISION REQUIRING LICENCE FROM GOVERNMENT OF CANADA TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN ANY IMPROVEMENT
speechtext: I think the hon. member for Medicine Hat has raised a point which has some merit; but at the same time, I am bound by the rule applying only to criticism of the conduct of a chairman. Perhaps nobody likes to raise a point of order when other members are being complimentary, and I think that is why objection is never taken to complimentary remarks made about chairmen from time to time even though the remarks are of a personal nature. But to get back to where I started, I have to advise the hon. member that criticism of the conduct of the chairman as such is not in order.

maintopic: PROVISION REQUIRING LICENCE FROM GOVERNMENT OF CANADA TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN ANY IMPROVEMENT
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I did not intend to say very much more about it. Possibly what I have said is sufficient. It is not my intention to outline the amendments that were proposed and accepted by the government. These have been very well covered by previous speakers. Nor will I take the time of the committee to place on record certain aspects of the evidence which I had previously intended to refer to at this particular stage of discussion of the bill. I still am of the opinion, however, that the

government is entering a field it has no business to enter and is claiming prerogatives outside its jurisdiction. I do not think I am the only one who feels that way.
During one of the first meetings of the committee it was agreed that notices would be sent to the various provincial governments stating that the bill was then before the committee, and expressing the thought that if they cared to send a delegation or make representations by letter that would be quite acceptable. The replies received were placed in the proceedings, and in reading them we find that some provincial authorities were not too happy with the purposes outlined in the bill. For instance, a reply was received from M. A. Patterson, attorney general of the province of Nova Scotia, which is found at page 31 of the proceedings of the committee. It is addressed to the chairman of the standing committee, and reads:
Retel March 2nd to Premier Hicks while I believe the constitutional validity of the proposed act is questionable I do not feel that the present is the proper time nor your committee the proper forum for the making of representations.
That is part of the telegram received from the government of Nova Scotia. We all understand and are well aware of the reaction of the government most concerned about the bill, the government of British Columbia. When notice was sent to the premier of that province the invitation was accepted and the committee was notified that a delegation would be sent to present a brief on behalf of the provincial government.
Then we find on pages 268 and 269 of the proceedings a communication from the premier of the province of Quebec, one paragraph of which reads as follows:
The government of the province of Quebec considers that the proposed federal legislation and the amendments in question are contrary to the rights and prerogatives of the province and that they constitute serious encroachments in the most important field of natural resources belonging to the province, particularly with reference to hydroelectric developments.
It will be seen that the views expressed by members of this group in the first debate on the measure were not just those of the individuals who expressed them, but also the opinions of some of the provinces. So I would submit that even after granting the concessions which have been granted, this government is still going beyond its rights in putting this bill through the committee. The authority for the type of development referred to in the bill covers an area composing over 22 per cent of British Columbia, and involves over 50 per cent of the hydro potential. We can readily understand, therefore, why the province is so jealous of its rights in connection with these matters.
International Rivers
The other day the hon. member for Eglinton referred to the fact that the people of Ontario would not look kindly on any endeavour to take control of the hydroelectric developments of Ontario. At the time I just wished the hon. member for Eglinton had been as ready to defend the particular project we have been discussing as he was to defend the project he was discussing at that particular time. We find that if this bill goes through not only the authority but also the responsibility will rest upon the federal government. They have chosen to set themselves up as the authority to license these particular projects. Now, I would feel that the responsibility is theirs to see that the province or provinces have access to the necessary capital to develop the resources for the good of the people of our country.
Now, Mr. Chairman, the picture of the possibilities of the development of the Columbia river basin as given by General McNaughton is almost staggering to the imagination. However, even though General McNaughton could not imagine himself being wrong about anything, it might be possible that some other authorities in some other governments could possibly be the repositories of at least a modicum of knowledge. I am not suggesting, of course-at least right at the moment-that General McNaughton is wrong. But I would like to suggest that even although to most of the government he is infallible, there may be the possibility that in some respects he may be slightly wrong.
In discussing this measure in committee the hon. member for Peace River, the leader of this group, tried to present the difficulties with which we were confronted in endeavouring to assess the effect of this particular measure and all that was involved in it. He called attention to some of the basic differences between General McNaughton and his advisers and the government of British Columbia and their advisers. I should like to refer to one particular instance at page 350 of the evidence of the committee. At the time Mr. Bonner was the witness, and we find this paragraph at the bottom of that page:

speechtext:
One of the questions which is uppermost in the minds of the provincial government in connection with the Castlegar dam is that the 3 million acre feet which it is proposed for storage should not be in excess of the 18-5 million which is noted on table 7 on page 71 of the proceedings of this committee. The 3 million which is in contemplation for lower Arrow lakes is not, as I am advised, to be considered over and above that 18,500,000 but rather is to be included in it. That is one of the premises under which the matter is being approached by the government of British Columbia.

That is something which we must insist upon for the proper development of the Columbia.
Then we turn to page 491 where the hon. member for Peace River was questioning General McNaughton. After reading the quotation which I have just read, the hon. member for Peace River said:
Now, the question then that I ask you first is this: You do not agree that the 3 million acre feet contemplated for lower Arrow lakes storage is contained within the 18.500,000?
A. No, sir, I most emphatically do not.
What right had General McNaughton to interpret something Mr. Bonner had said when Mr. Bonner made the plain statement that this was the premise from which the government was working? General McNaughton comes along and says that is not so. I would suggest, Mr. Chairman, we ought to consider some of the evidence submitted by General McNaughton. We ought to take a second look at it, because I think some of those statements were rather irresponsible for a man in his position.

speechtext: What was the use of trying?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources

speechtext: You never uttered a word in the committee.

maintopic: PROVISION REQUIRING LICENCE FROM GOVERNMENT OF CANADA TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN ANY IMPROVEMENT
speechtext:
What was the use? The government supporters took everything he said as gospel, and if anybody disagreed with that then they were entirely wrong.
The second observation I wish to make has to do with the suggested diversions of flood waters, especially of the flood waters of the Columbia into the Fraser. I understand there is another diversion from the Kootenay into the Columbia and then from the Columbia into the Fraser. This is for the purpose of hydroelectric projects on the Fraser. This question was raised both here and in the committee. In view of the great issues involved and the reports which continue to circulate, I suggest that the matter be given exhaustive study to determine beyond any question the effect any power developments on the Fraser may have upon the multimillion dollar fish industry on the Pacific coast.
I refer to the evidence that was given in this connection in the committee. At page 41 we find General McNaughton continuing with his statement, and he says:
This proposal has been considered by the fisheries experts, and they welcome the possibility of providing the Vancouver area with the power it needs, without at the same time having to put in a lot of high dams up which the fish cannot go. There is no objection to those proposals from the fisheries point of view, but discussions are going on.

On page 119 we have a further statement by General McNaughton:
Now, as regards the development itself and the danger to fish, and particularly the danger to the small fish going down, to which General Pearkes has referred, the danger becomes most important when you get to dams which have heads running above 200 feet. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to incorporate a pipe-line company under the provisions of the Pipe Lines Act. I think all members are aware of the fact that if any company desires to engage in the operation of a pipe line which crosses an interprovincial or the international boundary it must be incorporated by an act of parliament pursuant to the provisions of the Pipe Lines Act. After the bill has received third reading the matter must be referred to the board of transport commissioners, whose duty it is to investigate and inquire into the capitalization of the company, the need for the pipe line, the course it will follow, and so on.
Several bills of this type have been presented to the house this session, and it seems to me this bill follows closely the other pipeline bills that have been presented. I have compared the provisions of this bill with the provisions of other pipe-line bills, and it seems to me that it follows the usual pattern of the bills that have been presented. Probably the most important clause in the bill is clause 5, which follows the wording of similar clauses in other pipe-line bills. I should like to direct the attention of hon. members to clause 6 of the bill, which contains the following proviso:
Provided that the main pipe line or lines for the transmission and transportation of gas and oil shall be located entirely within Canada.
It is the intention of the incorporators of this company that this pipe line will be located entirely within this country and will not at any time enter the United States. The names of the applicants appear in clause 1 of the bill, and they constitute a well-balanced group of engineers, petroleum products specialists and contractors who are familiar with the financing, construction and operation of pipe-line projects. They do not intend to compete with large interprovincial lines; what they have in mind is the gathering up of the production of small wells in order to make these natural resources available to local communities.
IMr. St. Laurent.]
Were the gas and oil to be transported by truck or by railway tank car it would prove a most expensive procedure, and by establishing a pipe line the transportation can be carried out in a most inexpensive manner. The applicants propose to construct a pipe line to cross from the easterly part of Alberta to the westerly part of Saskatchewan. If the bill is given second reading I intend to move that it be referred to the proper standing committee where more detailed information can be provided.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, June 10, consideration of the motion of Mr. Argue for the second reading of Bill No. 22, to amend the Canada Grain Act, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Tucker.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR FAIR ALLOCATION OF BOX CARS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the fifth occasion on which this bill has been up for debate. Since the subject matter of the bill has been given a most thorough discussion in the house and before the agriculture committee I am hopeful that we may have a vote at this time. When the

bill was before the house last Friday the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) moved an amendment which, if passed, will kill the principle of the bill.
The purpose of introducing this bill is to restore to the producers in western Canada what I consider to be a fundamental Canadian right, namely the right to do their business with the elevator of their own choice. Year after year, in parliament and before the agriculture committee, members of the C.C.F. and representatives of western farm organizations have been endeavouring to get the government to do something to solve this problem and restore this right to western farmers.
Last session we thought something might be done when the minister promised to implement a car cycle at local points, but nothing came of it. Then we hoped that as a result of the further agriculture committee meetings this year this problem would be solved. Instead we have before the house a report which turns over the distribution of box cars to the Canadian wheat board without in any way providing that the farmers be given the right to deliver grain to the elevators of their own choice.
Then only last Friday the hon. member for Rosthern moved in amendment that the bill be not now read a second time but that instead the house reaffirm a paragraph taken from the report of the agriculture committee, naming the wheat board as an agency for the distribution of box cars. That is another attempt to avoid the issue. That is raising another phony excuse following a great many other phony excuses we have had in the past. I went over the many excuses advanced by the Minister of Trade and Commerce when I spoke last Friday. I was about to mention the last excuse he used, namely that the bill before the house was not constitutional. With regard to constitutionality the minister said, as reported on page 3756 of Hansard of May 13, the following:
The government has been advised to the contrary, not indeed with respect to this particular bill but with respect to other proposals for allocation of box cars which would govern competition between elevator companies.
We had the wheat pools before the agriculture committee advancing a solution to this problem. It was never suggested, to the best of my knowledge, before that committee that such a proposal was not constitutional. As a matter of fact I made a request that there should come before the agriculture committee a witness from the justice department to say whether or not this proposition was constitutional. No such witness was brought before the committee. I am therefore
Canada Grain Act
confident that this proposal is constitutional in every way. As a matter of fact, it is demonstrated now that the government has the constitutional power because the power to distribute box cars is being placed in the hands of the Canadian wheat board. So the excuses about constitutionality will in fact not stand the light of day.
This battle for the restoration to farmers of a fundamental right is not a new battle. It has been going on intermittently for 50 years. At various times producers have demanded what they believed to be a just right in the marketing of their grain. They have been refused from time to time by the government in power, but farm organizations and farmers continued to keep pressure on the government until a solution was obtained. Even though the government may refuse to solve this fundamental problem at this time, nevertheless farm organizations will continue to demand a solution. Pressure will build up, and some day the government is going to have to solve this problem.
The farmers of western Canada, in the words of the Saskatchewan wheat pool, are fighting mad that a fundamental right they have enjoyed for 50 years has been taken away from them. The fact that thousands of letters have come to members and to the government this session demanding a solution and that the government has done nothing will not discourage the producers of western Canada. There will be further letters; there will be further representations to the government. I suggest that unless this problem is solved the government may yet see another mass delegation of wheat farmers coming to Ottawa to demand this problem be solved and that a fundamental right be restored.
The government now is taking the jurisdiction over the distribution of box cars away from the railway companies, out from under the Canada Grain Act, and according to the recommendation of the agriculture committee are going to ask the Canadian wheat board to get into the business of box car distribution. The minister has said repeatedly that the Canadian wheat board's first business was to sell wheat and that the Canadian wheat board should not have to spend its time in the business of distributing box cars. We never disagreed with that statement; we always agreed with it. But now the minister is forcing the Canadian wheat board to undertake the distribution of box cars on the one hand, something the wheat board should not be doing and on the other hand something the farmer himself should control.
The agriculture committee has reported. The report is unanimous. But let no member

Canada Grain Act
of parliament think that the section recommending this new method of box car distribution is unanimous. That section is opposed by members of this group, because we feel it is something that will not work. It is wrong, because you are asking the wheat board to do something it should not be doing. It will not work, because the Canadian wheat board cannot give to the various elevator systems the exact percentage of box cars based on the wishes of the producers in western Canada.
Even if the Canadian wheat board distributes box cars to a local elevator point on the basis of the recommendations of the elevator companies, it will still be impossible for box cars to be distributed in an equitable manner. That is impossible because at a shipping point, for example, where you have four elevator companies you will have each company deciding the number of box cars that will go to its elevator at a given time. Any single company, by sending a certain number of box cars to its elevator at that point, will be able to get a greater percentage of grain than it would get if box cars were distributed on the basis of the farmer's own choice.
It is a shame that producers even now will not be allowed to take their business to the elevator they wish to patronize. I said in moving this measure more than live weeks ago that a cabinet minister would not like to be told that he would have to buy a Volkswagen if he wanted to buy a Cadillac. He would say, "If I have sufficient money to buy a Cadillac and I want to drive a Cadillac, that is the car I am going to buy". Why then should a farmer in western Canada be forced to deliver his grain to a certain elevator, because of the maldistribution of box cars?
Because we in this group believe this is something that should not continue, because we disagree with the amendment moved by the hon. member for Rosthern as it now stands, I wish to move, seconded by the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Johnson):
That the amendment be amended by deleting all the words after the words "shipping point" and substituting therefor the following words:
"according to the preference of producers at that point".
While I did not draft that amendment on the basis of the resolution passed by the Saskatchewan Liberal party in convention on September 23, 1954, I nevertheless find that the Saskatchewan Liberal party in convention passed a resolution in almost precisely the same terms, which reads as follows:
On the question of box car allocation, the convention urged that the Canada Grain Act be amended to provide for placing box cars at country elevators in accordance with the farmers' preference.

This subamendment would provide an instruction to the Canadian wheat board to distribute box cars in accordance with the preference of producers. It is because we believe in freedom of choice for the producers that we are moving this subamendment.
