Mr. Speaker, I almost feel like apologizing to the house for speaking once again on this question of box car distribution. However, in view of the extensive remarks that were made, particularly last Friday and again today, by the hon. member for Assiniboia on the recent proceedings of the committee on agriculture, I feel that I would be remiss in my duty as chairman, particularly, if I did not correct some of the statements.
As a matter of fact, I think this year the committee on agriculture did an extremely good job. We had an extensive discussion on the whole grain question. We dealt at length with this question which is now before the house. I think it is fair to say that at no time during the proceedings of the committee on agriculture this year did party politics muddy the waters throughout the discussion. I believe the committee gave serious, earnest and objective study to this whole question of box car distribution. After having given such a study, the committee unanimously agreed on a recommendation in order to try to solve this problem equitably.
Our C.C.F. friends, now that they are back in the house, on a bill previously moved are trying to explain their position in committee, I suggest, in the light of political ramifications. I must say that I was greatly disappointed in the speech made by the hon. member for Kindersley. Frankly, I may say that the hon. member attended assiduously at all the sittings of the agriculture committee. He seemed to be interested in the proceedings. I was amazed, however, at the interpretation he placed on the record of the evidence presented to the committee. Practically every paragraph of his speech of last Friday is either absolutely wrong or places a wrong interpretation on the evidence presented to the committee. I am sure a twelve-year-old who sat in the committee would have done a better job of interpreting the evidence than that which was done by the hon. member for Kindersley last Friday. I shall not be obliged to deal with the amendment that he suggested was moved in the committee because having heard the one that was moved today, I think I have heard it before and possibly there is a very great resemblance between the two. Hence if I deal with one I shall be dealing with the two at the same time.

At the same time I want to say, to begin with, that all this nonsense we have been hearing about the government or the Liberals or anybody else being opposed to giving the farmer the right to exercise his choice in the matter of delivery to elevators is just a red herring that has been drawn across the trail by the C.C.F. for the last two or three years. They have dragged it across the trail for so long that it is now beginning to stink. Naturally nobody is opposed to giving everyone his choice with regard to the elevator to which he delivers.

speechtext: Prove it when you vote.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR FAIR ALLOCATION OF BOX CARS
speechtext:
I shall do so in due time, and I will show you where you were wrong in many other instances in your speech the other day. You did not get the implication of the evidence at all during the sittings of that committee. One would have thought you had not been present at the meetings. I am sorry, Mr. Speaker; one should address the Chair. From reading the speech, Mr. Speaker, one would have thought the hon. member had not been present at any of the meetings.
Everybody has an earnest desire to try to solve this difficulty in the most practical way. Our C.C.F. friends say, "We want to give everybody the preference". Let me say this. I have a car, and there may be 25 people who want to get into my car. If they all want to get in at the same time, on the first trip, there is bound to be difficulty. I may ascertain their choice, but if they all want to get in first and if they keep on saying they all want to get in, it does not get them in the car because they will not be any better able to get into the car after expressing their preference than they were before. The question is how to provide transportation for all those people. That is the crux of the matter that this amendment is trying to solve.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR FAIR ALLOCATION OF BOX CARS
speechtext: Get a box car.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR FAIR ALLOCATION OF BOX CARS
speechtext:
Even a box car will not do it. I am tired of hearing the C.C.F. posing in this house and throughout the country, saying they are the only people in this country who are trying to help the farmers get the advantage of exercising their choice in the matter of delivery of their grain. Of course the whole committee was unanimous; everybody tried to find a solution to this problem. I venture to say
Canada Grain Act
that the pool organization will agree with me that this amendment will solve, if not all the problems, at least 95 per cent of them in the three western provinces.
The point is that even this amendment suggested by the hon. member for Assiniboia is not a serious one. It makes no effort to carry out the resolution. The preference is directed to the spotting of box cars. 1 shall not read the amendment and the subamendment, but the subamendment is directed at the distribution of box cars. The amendment is to the effect that the cars will be spotted according to the allocation of orders. Hence, even if you ascertain the preference at the box car level it will not solve the problem if the orders are not allocated differently. Even the hon. member for Kindersley, in his great confusion, admitted that principle last Friday. As reported at page 4658 of Hansard he made this statement:
The percentage of allocation among the elevator companies determines the ability of the farmers to deliver grain to the elevator of their choice.
That is the crux of the whole thing. Who does the allocating of the orders? It is the Canadian wheat board. So no matter what you do at the other level, unless you change the proportion of orders that go out to the various elevators it will not solve the problem in any way.
As to the complaints of the pool throughout the evidence, may I say this. Again the hon. member for Kindersley is wrong when he says that Mr. Wesson in his evidence said he did not know the proportion of allocations. It is quite true that he said he did not know what other companies were getting, but he admitted that he knew very well-and it is obvious that he would know-what percentage he was getting. If he knows what he is getting, and if they all know what they are getting-I refer to the three pools-then it is a simple arithmetical calculation to find out where the balance goes and whether company A or company B gets 20 per cent or 35 per cent is no concern of theirs. Another witness in the same position as Mr. Wesson admitted readily before the committee that he knew quite well what he was getting, and he said he had a very good idea what the others were getting.
At any rate, the percentage of grain that will move is determined, as you stated, by the amount of grain ordered by the Canadian wheat board. Without exception all the witnesses agreed that the wheat board had to have the right to order grain at the present time. They agreed this was a necessity that could not be helped. They agreed that it should have precedence over the car order book or any other scheme. The first requisite is for the wheat board to get a buyer, and the second step is to move the grain to a selling position. Consequently board orders had to be given preference over everything else.
The question arises of one elevator, one car, which the hon. member for Assiniboia again brought up last Friday. He said the minister was wrong, and by the same token I must have been wrong because I said the same thing previously, that the box cars were not spotted one elevator, one car. There again, what is the truth? It all came out in the committee. The hon. member for Assiniboia said the president of one of the pools read a letter from the board of grain commissioners. He was wrong, because the letter he read was from the railways. He read a letter from the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway. It is true that in that letter the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway said that as far as they were concerned they would allocate cars on the basis of one elevator, one car; but the same witness in the same breath-I believe he repeated it twice so there would be no misunderstanding-made it clear that in actual practice that was not what they were doing.
If you analyse the statistics presented to the committee you will find the facts of the matter are that a great many elevators at many points get a percentage which varies considerably. Consequently cars could not be spotted on the basis of one elevator, one car over the year. The answer of the main witness on that point was that they were not spotted on the basis of one elevator, one car

ultimately. You will recall all the discussion about the word "ultimately". He said that if there was any dispute at the beginning of the shipping orders it was one elevator, one car, and that when one elevator ran out of orders all the cars were sent to the elevator that had orders left.
This was their main complaint, and we agreed with that. That is why the committee recommended that cars should be spotted in the same proportion as orders are issued by the Canadian wheat board. It is quite clear that the hon. member for Assiniboia did not understand the report of the committee, and he does not understand the amendment now before the house. He says what we have done is ask the wheat board to distribute cars. The recommendation does not do that at all. It does not change the procedure one iota. It is exactly the same procedure as was followed last year.
The hon. member missed the point of the recommendation. The Canadian wheat board does not allocate cars and will not allocate cars. All the recommendation does is ask the wheat board to instruct the railways to spot cars, not ultimately but from the beginning, in the same proportion as shipping orders are issued by the board. If that is done I do not say it will solve all the problems, but it certainly should solve most of them.
Any amendment to the car order book that could be suggested at the moment would not help the present situation one iota, because we are operating now under special orders of the board and the car order book is not in operation. Therefore no matter what you do to the car order book section, no matter what bill you pass, no matter what amendment you make, it will not be operative because the car order book is out the window. Every witness before the committee said that the car order book was not operative. In my own province I believe it is operating at five points, and there only partially. I think Mr. Wesson said that in Saskatchewan it was not being operated at any point because they recognized the necessity of giving precedence to these shipping orders.

I am now going to say this, and I could have said it earlier. I believe this approach is sound. I think the government, with respect to their contribution to the municipalities, have a very fair precedent to go on in their formula introduced in 1949 respecting the payments in lieu of taxes on crown corporations or crown companies, such as Polymer in the city of Sarnia. I am quite satisfied of this. I hope I speak for others as I speak for the city of Sarnia when I say that formula has been regarded as very fair since it came into effect. The unfortunate part is that it was late coming in. Had we had the formula from the time Polymer was constructed, the city of Sarnia would have received probably $1 million between the time of its construction and the time payments were made in lieu of taxes.
I am now suggesting that that formula should apply to all crown property. While this is a step in the right direction, I sincerely hope that in another year the government will see fit to introduce further legislation so that no crown company property or no crown property in any part of Canada will be exempt from taxation. Or I might put it this way. I hope the government will see fit to introduce legislation so that all crown property will make payments in lieu of taxes on a basis that is fair and equitable, under the same principle that is applied to crown corporations.

I do not think there will be any disagreement by any member in the House of Commons on this point. Special provisions have been made for the city of Ottawa-and I say this with all deference to government policy-but up until the recent enactment whereby the city gets a greater share than it formerly received, these additional amounts that are now being paid by the government on its property were a burden, as you might say, on the small home owner. I do not think this government or any other government should, because of crown property, impose upon veterans or small home owners obligations which, after all, should be shared by all the taxpayers of the Dominion of Canada; and they would be so shared if crown property were to pay on the same basis as any individual or any company.
In connection with increased taxes I should like to refer to a problem I have mentioned before, which is not local but national. I refer to the increased cost of education. We will have to face the situation, because no one is going to agree to any suggestion that we lower our standards of education. In the last ten years it has doubled or trebled. While the measure before us will alleviate to a certain extent the heavy responsibility of small home owners to their municipalities, I submit that additional legislation should be introduced at the earliest possible moment to make all crown properties subject to the same payments to municipalities as are now applicable to crown companies. I trust the government will consider it advisable to do so.

Mr. Chairman, there are three minor points I wish to mention at this time. I notice that the resolution does not completely meet the desires of municipal officials across Canada in that it still provides a loophole or means whereby the minister is able to compensate municipalities on a lesser scale than if the municipalities were given outright powers to tax real estate owned by the federal government. I see no reason whatsoever why the federal government should not pay its full share of the municipal tax load on any real estate it owns within the borders of a municipality. In the western part of Canada at least the provincial governments are very slowly coming around to

assuming their share of the municipal tax load on property they hold within municipalities, and I think the federal government is being just a little slow in acknowledging its responsibility. We often ponder ways and means of helping municipalities. Here is one way we could help them much more than we are doing now, and we would be able to do so without violating any constitutional provision or any other prohibition that may be in the way.
There is another matter I think should be raised at this time. I refer to the burden imposed upon municipalities by people building houses or shacks on federally-owned land within a municipality. We usually call these people squatters, although they may or may not like to have that name applied to them. However, these people add to the burden of the social welfare departments of the municipalities concerned. I think the federal government has a responsibility here. They should either move these people into adequate housing somewhere else, housing these people are able to afford, or they should compensate the municipalities for, in some cases, the hundreds of squatters who are allowed to live on federally-owned land and become a burden to the municipalities in which these federal lands are located. I think it is an unfair imposition to allow people to live on these lands.
Another cause of worry to some municipalities arises out of land held by the federal government that is not being properly looked after. In the middle of a rapidly growing suburban or metropolitan area you may have an acre of land which is crown property owned by the federal government. Possibly it was purchased 40 or 50 years ago as the site of a potential federal building. Perhaps its purchase was the result of an election pledge away back in 1911 or around that time. Everybody in the city uses this vacant land as a garbage dump, and again there is an imposition on the municipality because it has to maintain the appearance of the property and look after the upkeep of this federal real estate. I think such real estate should either be disposed of on the market or the municipality should be given adequate compensation for looking after it so it does not depreciate the value of nearby property.

Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CERTAIN BENEFITS
speechtext: Is the parliamentary assistant going to make a statement?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CERTAIN BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a short statement in respect to these amendments. It is proposed to amend the Prairie Farm Assistance Act to, one, make provision for payments on land which cannot be seeded or summerfallowed on account of natural causes beyond the farmer's control; and, two, require that the blocks of six or more sections which are excluded from payment, or paid, under section 6, be rectangular in shape instead of irregular.
Over widespread areas in the prairie provinces these last few years it has been impossible to seed, and in some cases even to summerfallow, lands which had been farmed for many years. It is considered that


such lands should qualify for assistance under the act the same as other lands do at present.
At present the act provides for the exclusion from payment within eligible townships of certain blocks of six or more sections which had an average yield of ten or more bushels of wheat and for the payment within ineligible townships of similar blocks which had an average yield of less than eight bushels. Prior to 1950 the act required that such blocks be rectangular in shape, but this requirement was removed that year. Since that time, and particularly during the last crop year, administrative difficulties have arisen in many instances when setting up irregular blocks, in that discriminatory distinctions as between neighbours show up to an extent not foreseen when the amendments were made. It is therefore proposed to revert to the provisions regarding these blocks of sections as they were prior to the 1950 amendment.
As it has been impossible to seed or cultivate over widespread areas this year these amendments should be made effective for the 1955 crop season, and it is desirable that they be introduced at the present session of parliament.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CERTAIN BENEFITS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not know what is in the bill that will follow this resolution, but if it contains anything that will help the farmers in my district I certainly welcome it and will be glad to see it pass.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CERTAIN BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the part of the announcement by the parliamentary assistant that land that cannot be seeded because of natural causes will be eligible for prairie farm assistance is welcome, but that portion of the announcement that the provision with regard to six sections will be changed from the present provision whereby the block of sections need only be contiguous and not necessarily rectangular is a backward step.
I would like to have seen a really important amendment made to this act, namely to increase the size of the payment. The act is a good act, but nothing has been done about the size of the payment since it was first passed in 1939. I see the Minister of National Health and Welfare smiling, and I know he will recall that I used the same argument in reference to family allowances, which come under his department.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CERTAIN BENEFITS
speechtext: I was smiling at something else.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CERTAIN BENEFITS
speechtext:
The Prairie Farm Assistance Act passed in 1939 provided for a maximum payment in time of crop failure of $500. The purchasing power of $500 in 1939 would

perhaps equal that of $1,200 today, so if the Prairie Farm Assistance Act is to be made as valuable in 1955 as it was in the late thirties, when first passed by this parliament, the size of the payment will have to be more than doubled.
Certainly we welcome any provision that brings in areas which have been flooded. The farmer who is unable to seed his land because of flooding should be considered under the act to have had a crop failure on that acreage.
I take it that is the provision to be written into the act, and with that we are certainly in agreement.
The six-section provision, that it is to be made a rectangular block of land, in my opinion merely means that more farmers having high yields will be getting the bonus when they should not be entitled to it because they do not need it, and more farmers who have a crop failure in the sense that they have a yield of less than four bushels to the acre in one category or less than eight bushels to the acre in another category will be denied the bonus. The more irregular the area on which the payment can be made the more likely it is that the farmer with a crop failure will receive the payment.
Another provision which I should like to see in the bill is the deletion of subsection 3 of section 3 of the act, namely that part of the act which bars certain crown lands which have been disposed of since 1940. There is some merit in doing everything possible to see that submarginal lands are not made eligible for prairie farm assistance, but to discriminate against land merely because it was in the name of the crown previous to 1940, although it may be as good grain-producing land as there is in any part of western Canada, is not fair.
When the minister presented this proposal some years ago he intended to take out a great deal more land than was finally taken out. The bill proposed at that time went to the agriculture committee, and the minister put back under the act much of the land that he intended to take out. My only regret is that he did not go all the way and put it all back under the act, so that all land might be eligible no matter whether it had been in the name of the crown previous to 1940 or not. We shall look at the bill when we receive it, and perhaps at that time discuss it in more detail.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CERTAIN BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the proposal to change back to a rectangle the shape of the block of six sections I think perhaps is a good amendment, because it has caused a tremendous amount of hard feeling and hardship in the past. When the department would
Blind Persons Act
establish a block of six sections within a township as being eligible, this often denied farmers in those six sections the right to receive the bonus.
Of course where the purpose is to establish a block of six sections in an ineligible township for the purpose of allowing those six sections to obtain the bonus, then the change will be to the disadvantage of the farmer. On the other hand, if we take six sections out the change will help the farmer. If you propose to establish a block of six sections, it will deny certain farmers the benefit they might otherwise receive. But I believe on the whole that it works both ways, whether you take a block in or out and, in the long run, it will be a good thing to make the change. As the parliamentary assistant has pointed out, it is very difficult to explain to farmers that they should be denied the bonus when their neighbours are receiving it. They do not understand that a block has been formed in the shape of a pair of steps, and it does not make sense to them. It will be easier to explain to them when it is back in a rectangular block. Some farmers will lose as a result of the change and some will gain. On balance I do not see that there will be any disadvantage to it.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in.

Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS LOWERING ELIGIBLE AGE TO 18 YEARS AND INCREASING MAXIMUM ANNUAL INCOMES
speechtext:
I
just want to rise to say that we on this side

Blind Persons Act
of the house give wholehearted support to this bill but, like other hon. members, we would prefer to see the age limit for the recipients lowered. The family allowance stops at 16. We feel that blind persons should be given this allowance at 16 rather than 18. That two-year period between 16 and 18 can be the most expensive of all for blind persons. It is certainly the most expensive period in the educational life of a normal student, and how much more so it must be for a blind person.
The minister has explained that 18 is the eligible age for disabled persons. Under the Blind Persons Act it was 21. Bringing the age down to 18 means that blind persons are being put on the same basis as disabled persons. The minister indicated that the age could not be lowered for blind persons unless it was also lowered for disabled persons. That, of course, is a fair way of looking at it; but it just so happens that we are discussing a bill to amend the Blind Persons Act.
I feel that Canadians would be making a good investment in lowering the eligible age to 16, an investment that would help blind persons to help themselves. Those hon. members who have had anything to do with blind persons know that a special measure of courage and cheerfulness seems to be bestowed upon them. They themselves strive for an independence which is inspirational to all of us; and I am sure the minister will agree with that. Last year I watched a golf tournament of blind persons, and it was an unforgettable experience. I do not think any golfers ever enjoyed themselves more.
More recently I called upon Canada's famous spokesman for all blind persons in this country, Colonel Eddie Baker, head of the Canadian National Institute for the Blind. Colonel Baker was himself blinded in world war I and since then has devoted his life to the rehabilitation of blind persons. It was before the minister had brought this bill to the house that I called on Colonel Baker, and the purpose of my visit was quite removed from this bill or the fact that I might some day speak on this subject. I had heard that Colonel Baker had a workshop in his basement and I wanted to see that workshop. I never saw more vicious looking tools, and to watch that man handicapped by blindness pursuing a hobby that sighted people could not enjoy more was a great inspiration to me. Blindness has not deterred him in his choice of a hobby or in his usefulness to Canadian citizens.
I mention these two things because I feel they emphasize the spirit of independence with which blind people face life. They do 
not sit back and say the world owes them a living. They want to earn their own living, and they want to make their own contribution to life. I feel that we who have eyes to see have a great debt to these people who do not ask anything of us. I feel we must hold out a helping hand with generosity.
The hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair) suggested that a guiding allowance should be granted, and this suggestion also came from the Canadian Council for the Blind. I hope in future the Minister of National Health and Welfare will look with favour on this suggestion. I know he is sympathetic in these matters, and I am in no way offering any criticism. I am just expressing my own and my party's tribute to these people who make a great contribution as Canadian citizens.
There is unanimous support in this house also for an increase in the maximum annual income. I should like to see the bill go even further. I should like to see us put the maximum annual income at the very top for these people. I hope the minister will take another look at that suggestion in the not too far distant future. I congratulate the minister upon this bill. I hope that before very long he will accept and have enacted the further suggestions that have been made from this side of the house.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS LOWERING ELIGIBLE AGE TO 18 YEARS AND INCREASING MAXIMUM ANNUAL INCOMES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for York-Humber (Miss Aitken) has just indicated, when legislation improving our enactments respecting the blind is brought before us, that legislation has the unanimous support of this house. While the hon. member made that statement with reference to one particular aspect of the bill, I do not think I am being unfair to her when I take it that the members of her party and of all parties in this house are happy to see any improvement at all in the legislation affecting the lot of the blind people of this country, so this bill will pass this house unanimously.
We welcome the reduction in the eligible age. We too feel that this age should be set at 16 rather than 18. In other words it should be at the point where the family allowance breaks off. Indeed, we made that same point with respect to the disability allowance. We also feel that the limits of income allowed to the blind, which this bill increases to a certain extent, might not only be raised to the highest possible limit, as was suggested by the hon. member for York-Humber, but indeed that this is a piece of legislation with respect to which the means test might be abolished altogether.

I know there are those who still bring forth arguments in defence of means tests in certain cases. But I remind hon. members that we have in this country a few pieces of social legislation from which means test provisions have been removed. I think in particular of the Old Age Security Act and the Family Allowances Act, under both of which payments under the heading of social security are made to Canadians without any means test. So far as those under old age security are concerned where persons are already in receipt of substantial income, the answer is that any additional income that comes from a means-test-free old age pension is subject to income tax. If there are those who want to argue that there are a few blind persons who are fortunate enough to have a bit of income, I would point out that the payment of a means-test-free pension to them would be treated in the same way.
Actually we know there are not many of these persons who are able to earn an income of any size; rather the fact of the matter is that even with all the spirit and initiative these people have they are under a handicap that I feel we might well recognize by the payment of a blindness allowance or blind pension without any means test whatsoever.
I am satisfied that the day will come when we will remove the means test from the Blind Persons Act. I urge the government to give the matter favourable consideration and not to let that day be too far in the future.
While speaking in support of this resolution I also wish to indicate that we feel that consideration should have been given to the request of organizations representing the blind for a guidance allowance. I hope that even yet that request will be considered and met by the government.
So, Mr. Speaker, I conclude with these few word's indicating our keen desire to do anything we can to help these people, and indicating that, while we feel that there are further improvements that should be made with the least possible delay, we are nevertheless glad to give our full support to the second reading of Bill No. 350.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I quite agree with what has been said by the last two hon. members who have spoken. The fact that the family allowance stops at the age of 16 years and that there is a gap between 16 and 18 is not the only reason the age limit should be reduced to 16 years. It should be reduced to that age for this reason also. Persons who are blind must learn the different things they can be taught when they are young. When they get older and get into set ways, it is hard to
Blind. Persons Act
get them to learn and in many cases they will not be taught. When they are 16 years of age, or between the ages of 16 and 18, their fingers are sensitive and they can be taught braille quite easily. At that age they also must have a typewriter, which costs money, as does the equipment for that typewriter.
There are also braille slates to be bought. Just within the last year in the United States a drawing board has been brought out and developed by an American. It is a plastic slate. On top of that slate there is rubber. On top of that rubber is placed a cellophane sheet. The blind person can draw on that slate and when it is turned over he can feel the outline of that drawing; or on it a person who has sight can give a blind person directions as to streets and one thing and another, and it can be turned over and the blind person can follow them. All these things cost money. The blind person is therefore put to quite a bit of expense.
Just lately-within the last six months or so, or perhaps less than that-the talking books that are distributed to blind persons who have these talking book machines have been changed. There is a new needle that must be used on these machines. In order to use these talking books these blind people must have a machine that has an arm on it so that they can turn it. I am not sure whether it is a 78 r.p.m. needle or a different kind of needle. However, there are two kinds of records. If you use the wrong needle it will spoil the record. All these new records that are coming out are marked with the letter "M" on them. It is a large, raised letter so blind people can feel and read it.
What I am getting at is the fact that these talking books and all this equipment run into money. I doubt whether a blind person could afford to buy these things unless his parents or some friend were able to buy them for him. I therefore feel that this age limit should be reduced to 16 years so the blind person would have that extra money with which to go on and be better prepared when he became 18 years of age.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS LOWERING ELIGIBLE AGE TO 18 YEARS AND INCREASING MAXIMUM ANNUAL INCOMES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to associate myself and my colleagues in the Social Credit group with the expressions of approval of the bill now before us. The amendment is certainly welcome and is long overdue. I have noticed with a great deal of interest that there are times in the house when all members of parliament, irrespective of political affiliation, do agree. Especially is that agreement evident when we have before us legislation that has as its purpose and intent to assist those who are heavily handicapped. I like to interpret that type of unanimity not only as indicating the proper discharge of our traditional responsibilities but also, and perhaps more important, as expressing in a certain sense a prominent characteristic of our Canadian people, their concern that all men in high office should take a generous attitude toward those who are heavily handicapped and in distress.

We certainly welcome the amendment and see in it protection for those who hitherto have not been covered. In our debates we often make comparisons in order to justify certain accomplishments that Canada has achieved. It is done during debates on agricultural problems. We compare our surpluses with those of other nations. The same thing happens with respect to housing legislation. We compare it with that of other countries. But as far as social legislation is concerned I think we should adopt the attitude that our legislation should not be compared with that of some other country but should in fact be a model for other nations to emulate.
I should certainly like to see steps taken soon to protect those now unprotected, namely the group between the ages of 16 and 18. I am not a pediatrician or child psychologist, but it seems to me that is the very age when sensitive minds become conscious of handicaps. I believe it is during that period that certain curative steps can be taken. It is between the ages of 16 and 18 that proper education and further training are so necessary for the handicapped child.
Furthermore, I understand that when a recipient of the blind allowance reaches the age of 70 he automatically comes within the old age security bracket and receives his pension on the same basis as those receiving old age security pensions. All things being equal, I think everybody in the house will admit that a person who is blind has an extra burden to bear, and I believe it is well within the realm of possibility for us to provide an extra measure of security for these people. Ordinarily many persons over 70 years of age who are not handicapped by blindness are able to supplement their earnings with useful work, but that is hardly the case with respect to persons handicapped by blindness. I think possibly the next thing we should concentrate on is extending the coverage and making a worth-while effort in the field of eye research.
We support the measure, not only because we think it is right but because we think Canada can well afford it. We are one of the richest countries in the world. We have only 15 million people, and I believe our social legislation can be made such that it will be second to none. We support the legislation and trust it will bring a certain measure of joy to those who hitherto have been handicapped and unprotected. We hope they will see in the amendment some reason for them to look to their future with confidence.

We all appreciate the motives behind the observations of the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Fraser) who, more than any other member in the house, has a personal reason for appreciating the advantages of this bill.
I should note, as the minister sponsoring the measure, that we seek to do two things. We seek first to increase the permissible outside income and second to lower the age. With regard to increasing the income ceilings, the amendment before the house will have some important results for all beneficiaries. A number of them now receiving only a partial allowance will have that allowance increased by as much as $10 to $20 a month. Most of them will actually receive the full allowance of $40.
A single blind person will be able to have outside income of $40 a month and still draw full allowance. His outside income will have to reach $80 a month before he goes off the allowance altogether. A married blind person with sighted spouse will be able to receive the full allowance of $40 even though the outside income of the couple reaches as high as $90 a month. Only when the outside income of the married couple exceeds $130 a month will the blind person cease to be eligible for even a partial allowance. A married couple who are both blind may both receive the full allowance, a total of $80, and still have outside income of $60 a month.
Besides increasing the allowance for those who receive partial benefits, this liberalization of income ceilings will add an unknown number, possibly as many as 500, new beneficiaries now excluded by the present ceiling. The lowering of the age from 21 to 18 follows a previous step of lowering the age from 40 to 21. The reason for keeping the age at 18 is that, as the hon. member for Lanark has noted, this is in keeping with disability legislation generally.

We are, therefore, aware of the work of the Canadian National Institute for the Blind and all the other organizations for the blind in our country, who do so much for this group of disabled citizens.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no particular quarrel with the amendments being introduced to the Canada Elections Act in the bill now before us, but I do feel that hon. members should realize that even with these proposed amendments our elections act as it will then stand will still leave in existence a situation under which a good many electors of this country are able to exercise their franchise in a federal election only under extreme difficulty, if at all. It has been said that the amendments are not of major importance and possibly the only solution to the problem I have in mind would require an amendment of major importance.
I believe I referred to this situation in the first speech I made in this house. It is a situation which exists in areas where working people are often required, in the pursuit of their normal occupations, to move from time to time and from place to place. I suggested at that time that with the industrial development of our country this is a situation which in the more remote areas is apt to be one of increasing importance to an increasing number of Canadians. Perhaps I might just give an illustration of the situation I have in mind.
I think I can describe it best by referring to what has happened in the area which I represent. Many hon. members will realize that there are a number of logging camps in my constituency, and I know of situations where camps have closed down between the time of enumeration and election day. Those camps provided the only place of residence the workers had at the time of enumeration.

Once the camps are closed down the living quarters, cook-houses and so on are closed down as well, and those people who have been enumerated as living in that particular polling area may have to move completely out of the constituency. In effect they are placed in the position that they are disfranchised.
The same applies to many people on the west coast engaged in the fishing industry. When an election is called at the height of the fishing season in many cases it means travelling many miles to return to the place where they are registered as voters. I know that many fishermen feel strongly on this matter of being virtually disfranchised under our present elections act.
I have given a good deal of thought to this matter, and the only practical suggestion as to how it could be overcome that I have been able to come up with is that we will have to introduce into the Canada Elections Act some provision for absentee voting. This provision has been in the British Columbia provincial elections act for many years and I believe has worked very well, without too many complications, except during that time when we had what was known as the single transferable vote.
This provision enables any elector in a provincial election in British Columbia to go into any polling place in the province and vote for the candidate of his own choice in his own riding.
Canada Elections Act
I realize that there may be a good many practical difficulties in the way of introducing such a plan into our federal elections act. I feel, however, that it could be successfully applied within constituencies within the boundaries of any one particular province. I feel that, before a federal election rolls around, this is a matter which could very well be given further consideration for incorporation in our federal elections act. I did not want to allow this bill to receive second reading without again drawing the attention of the house to the existence of this particular situation.

3.	Results of renegotiations initiated by Canada.
(See resolutions tabled by the Minister of Finance on June 2, 1955)
In compensation for the withdrawal of the concessions on ethylene glycol for antifreeze and on canned mixtures of fruit containing peaches, pears or apricots, the Canadian rate on canned peaches is being reduced from 2$c to 2c per pound; the rate on melons covered by tariff item 95(a) is being reduced from 2c to free; the rate on anti-freezing compounds of ethylene glycol base is being reduced from 20 per cent to 15 per cent; the rate on engines for power mowers is being reduced from 20 per cent to 15 per cent, and free entry for dental engines, chairs and dental units is being bound.
